section: Future Research and Management Practices Needed
subsection: Overview
claim_paragraph: Across the literature on agricultural subsurface (tile) drainage, authors converge on a consistent message: while individual practices and processes are increasingly well characterised, the field still lacks the long-term, multi-scale, and economically grounded evidence needed to design, target, and deploy cost-effective nutrient-mitigation strategies at the landscape scale. This section synthesises the research frontier around several recurring lines of inquiry. First, there is a widespread call for longer-duration, multi-year, and multi-site monitoring to smooth climatic variability and capture the true magnitude of system responses \parencite{Randall2003,Randall2005,Waring2024,Jeong2018,Cooke2012}. Second, nitrogen management remains a primary focus for refinement of application rates, timing, and decision-support tools \parencite{Christianson2015b,Bandura2025,Liu2021}. Third, phosphorus transport in subsurface drainage is repeatedly flagged as under-studied relative to its importance, particularly for dissolved and bioavailable fractions \parencite{Hertzberger2019,Yuan2022,deOliveira2022}. Fourth, a strong theme is that no single best management practice (BMP) is a "silver bullet": bundling in-field, edge-of-field, and water-management practices, and targeting them to hydrologically active critical source areas, is essential **[CITATION CHECKED: Baulch2019]**. Finally, authors emphasise that biophysical understanding must be coupled with economics, incentive design, policy reform, modelling advances, and stakeholder engagement before mitigation can be scaled \parencite{Liu2021,Kvítek2023,David2015}. The subsections below organise these open questions and priorities in turn, retaining the specific quantitative targets, methods, and conditions proposed by the source studies.

section: Future Research and Management Practices Needed
subsection: Bundling, sequencing, and edge-of-field practices
claim_paragraph: Region-specific bundling agendas reinforce this. \textcite{Baulch2019} lay out a broad cold-region research programme: investigating drainage effects on nutrient export under diverse weather while comparing surface, tile, and undrained fields; studying controlled drainage, channel design, and maintenance through wet--dry cycles; assessing rotational and spring tillage with altered nutrient management in reduced-till systems; determining net effects of perennial-forage conversion (stand age, composition, snowmelt infiltration); quantifying nutrient retention and remobilisation in reservoirs, wetlands, ponds, and buffers; refining nutrient management by minimising late-fall and winter applications and targeting hydrologically connected hotspots; and developing tile-drainage mitigation (controlled drainage, bioreactors, physico-chemical amendments) suited to snowmelt hydrology. \textcite{Gupta2023} call for more robust, cost-effective BMPs to aid cover-crop benefits and for robust edge-of-field BMPs to mitigate climate warming. \textcite{Husk2024} suggest wider application of agricultural bioreactors, P reactors, controlled drainage, and municipal low-impact development, potentially alongside internal-loading management such as sediment dredging, P inactivation, biomanipulation, aeration, and nutrient precipitation. **[CITATION CHECKED: HernandezRamirez2011]** and \textcite{GAYNOR1995b} point to intercrops and management that enhances crop nutrient uptake and alters watershed hydrology as promising for P-transport reduction, with tillage options beyond ridge and zero tillage still to be investigated. Edge-of-field structure research is also called for: quantifying gains from individual components of saturated riparian buffers, installing monitoring wells and backflow valves, and clarifying suspended-solids sources \parencite{Singh2024b}, and confirming that saturated-buffer N removal increases as buffer vegetation matures \parencite{Jaynes2019}. \textcite{Spiese2023} call for novel BMPs to address both nitrate and DRP simultaneously.

section: Future Research and Management Practices Needed
subsection: Long-term, multi-scale monitoring and experimental design
claim_paragraph: Experimental-design refinements are proposed alongside longer records. \textcite{Schilling2013} recommend establishing a suitable correlation among paired basins across a range of climate conditions, restricting paired sampling to the March--July period when most water and nitrate flows occur, delaying post-BMP monitoring to enhance the likelihood of detecting change, and using BMPs capable of achieving at least the minimum detectable change. \textcite{Sunohara2016} argue that BMP impacts on downstream receptors should be assessed simultaneously at multiple scales, from field to watershed. **[CITATION CHECKED: Irvine2019]** call for within-field and within-plot studies to elucidate the mechanistic processes responsible for nutrient export at the sub-watershed scale, and for additional field-scale studies within high-export sub-watersheds. \textcite{Xin2016c} recommend further experiments under a wider range of conditions to test the applicability of derived effective-yield formulas and models, while \textcite{Xiong2025} call for refined $^{15}$N loss observation and larger trial areas more representative of actual production, and \textcite{Loper2024} see mesocosms as an opportunity to quantify nutrient-loss responses to management changes.

section: Future Research and Management Practices Needed
subsection: Nitrogen management: rates, timing, tools, and loss pathways
claim_paragraph: Timing and method of application are recurring open questions. **[CITATION CHECKED: Liang2018]** propose combining timing with rate to further optimise N management and note the value of models such as WHCNS for evaluating short- and long-term drainage, N-loss, and crop-growth effects. \textcite{Hertzberger2019} call for additional coordinated field research on nutrient timing, note the continuing evolution of the MANAGE database as a research resource, and emphasise the need for greater research on P transport in subsurface drainage. \textcite{Malone2007b} highlight the need for more research to confidently quantify differences between split and single spring N applications and to check possible over-prediction of winter nitrification and N loss for fall manure on soybean. \textcite{HernandezRamirez2011} note it remains unknown whether reduced-rate fall manure could match sidedress or preplant applications environmentally, and point to nitrification inhibitors, winter cover crops, more complex rotations, and multifunctional landscapes as additional mitigation avenues, with controlled drainage as a supplementary method. \textcite{Elmi2005} stress the need to quantify all major N loss pathways simultaneously and to obtain better information on the relative merits of manure versus mineral management systems.

section: Future Research and Management Practices Needed
subsection: Economics, incentives, policy, adoption, and stakeholder engagement
claim_paragraph: A consistent frontier is that biophysical understanding alone is insufficient; economic evaluation, incentive design, policy reform, and farmer engagement are decisive for adoption. \textcite{Liu2021} call for advanced case-by-case cost analyses to guide policymakers, farm owners, and researchers, and for inter-agency action to promote 4R implementation. \textcite{Yuan2022} note more data are needed on the cost-effectiveness and ecological benefits of ACPs. **[CITATION CHECKED: McLellan2015]** plan to incorporate practice costs and cost-effectiveness into future work. \textcite{Christianson2014} recommend continued positive incentives such as CREP funding for wetlands (given high public and lower perceived private benefit), more information and educational programmes to increase adoption (especially for crop rotation), and greater consideration of broader-scale, non-excludable benefits in multifunctional landscapes. \textcite{David2015} argue that incentivising on-farm research and collaboration among farmers, programmes that generate a collective sense of conservation need, and scaling individual efforts to meso- and macro-scale policy are essential. \textcite{Jaynes2012} and \textcite{Karlen2005} both call for cost-share and risk-insurance mechanisms to raise adoption. \textcite{Kvítek2023} call for reassessment of legislation and revised incentives for the 2024+ period to remove barriers to natural-water-retention-measure adoption. \textcite{Marja2013} recommend national policy change to retain open ditch-and-field networks where subsurface drainage prevails, noting that removing state support for ditch replacement may suffice, with targeted agri-environmental support as an additional incentive in high-revenue regions. \textcite{Ghane2021b} identify nutrient-trading programmes as needed to increase shallow-drain adoption.

section: Future Research and Management Practices Needed
subsection: Cropping systems, cover crops, perennials, and land use change
claim_paragraph: Perennial and land-use-change options feature prominently. \textcite{Huang2023} suggest that gaining additional soil organic carbon may require purposeful management, that poorly drained depressions may be good candidates for conversion to perennial bioenergy crops such as \textit{Miscanthus $\times$ giganteus}, or restoration to wetlands by obstructing tile drains and planting native species. **[CITATION CHECKED: Norberg2022]** conclude that mitigating N losses is most effectively achieved by keeping soil covered year-round with a growing crop such as perennial ley, while the focus for P should be on decreasing surface runoff. \textcite{Arrueta2025} call for additional data on alfalfa's effect on subsurface discharge during large events, across diverse management and geographies, and better understanding of how nutrient and transport factors couple to govern temporal variability in export. \textcite{Djiemon2019} argue for better cropping practices to ensure long-term subsoiling returns, integrating cover crops and autumn cereals to dry soils in spring, and controlling machinery traffic and weight. \textcite{Woodbury2018} call for research on the value and payments for other externalities (P and sediment reduction, greenhouse-gas mitigation, biodiversity), which may further highlight switchgrass benefits when replacing maize. \textcite{Siksnane2017} list a suite of measures warranting evaluation: fertilisation planning and nutrient balancing, converting arable land to grassland, intercultural cultivation, winter crop farming, controlled drainage, organic farming, buffer-zone creation, and artificial wetlands with phytoremediation. \textcite{GARDNER1992} recommend greater emphasis on soil types beyond red-brown earths, increased subsoil root growth, deep ripping and deep placement of nutrients and gypsum, crop species that open subsoils, and lucerne in dryland systems with rotational grazing. \textcite{Oquist2007} note more research across regions is needed to determine whether conversion to alternative farming practices improves water quality elsewhere.

section: Future Research and Management Practices Needed
subsection: Phosphorus transport processes and mitigation research gaps
claim_paragraph: Phosphorus in subsurface drainage is repeatedly identified as under-researched relative to nitrogen. \textcite{Hertzberger2019} explicitly call for greater research effort on P transport in subsurface agricultural drainage and better understanding of nutrient-related water-quality issues. \textcite{Yuan2022} note that more research is needed on conservation-practice effectiveness in reducing dissolved-P loss from agricultural fields, particularly in subsurface flow, and on the causes of annual variability in reduction rates. \textcite{Pease2018} identify increasing understanding of the pedologic factors influencing P transport in subsurface-drained landscapes, and the effect of management on P loss, as key research needs across the Eastern Corn Belt, requiring examination of individual and combined management factors. **[CITATION CHECKED: deOliveira2022]** recommend refining P-loss frameworks through additional within-field studies, continued data collection on soil testing, site history, agronomic management, and water-quality/flow monitoring, and better understanding of the "where" and "when" of drainage P loss to sharpen conservation-practice timing and placement for disproportionate, targeted benefit.

section: Future Research Needs for Crop-Drainage Systems
subsection: Irrigation, salinity, and water reuse in arid and saline systems
claim_paragraph: Water-productivity and technology questions also recur. \textcite{Feng2019} propose using their outputs to design irrigation schedules under different hydrological years and soil water-salt environments and using the coupled HYDRUS--EPIC model to evaluate the future sustainability of saline-water irrigation. \textcite{Jia2017} recommend measuring water-table changes and their contribution to storage and evapotranspiration, recomputing water-application efficiency per day between soil samplings to account for water-table rise, reformulating the efficiency equation, and using longer irrigation durations or slower flow rates to improve uniformity. \textcite{Qin2025} call for scalable data-management infrastructures for long-term field deployment (energy-efficient edge computing, low-power IoT protocols), life-cycle cost and return-on-investment assessment under varying market and climate conditions, integration of agronomic models with environmental and economic frameworks in a unified precision-agriculture platform, and low-temperature crystallization to treat brine toward near-zero discharge. \textcite{Abdelkrim2021} note that specific irrigation dates and amounts should be scheduled using criteria beyond modeling, such as farmers' expert knowledge and sensors. **[CITATION CHECKED: DINAR1989]** call for a more complete economic evaluation of shifting irrigation technology including associated management variables, and \textcite{Qian2025} highlight the need to study solute transport during cultivation from a components perspective and to test applicability under drip irrigation. \textcite{ElHassanin2022} suggest that established thresholds could seed large-scale modeling or the development of water/drainage-management measures to raise field water-use fraction, crop-water productivity, and wheat production, and \textcite{RADSTAKE1988} recommend continued monitoring of crop yield and water-quality change to improve forecasts of groundwater suitability for irrigation in the Nile Valley. \textcite{Ayars2006} note that extending their method to other crops will require additional studies, and \textcite{Karegoudar2022} advise that policymakers may proceed under all three water-availability scenarios. Forage-water-use comparisons remain open: \textcite{Mundy2006} judge a comparison of the water-use efficiency of forages under flood versus spray irrigation worthwhile, and \textcite{Greenwood2006} defer forage yield and plant--soil--water responses to companion papers.

section: Future Research Needs for Crop-Drainage Systems
subsection: Overview
claim_paragraph: The literature on agricultural subsurface (tile) drainage converges on a shared meta-conclusion: despite decades of field and modeling work, the interactions among crop yield, nitrogen and phosphorus losses, and the field water balance remain insufficiently characterized across the full range of soils, climates, cropping systems, and drainage management practices that occur in tile-drained agriculture. Authors repeatedly frame future needs around \emph{extending scope} --- to more sites, soils, climates, crops, and longer observation periods --- and around \emph{sharpening the tools} used to synthesize and extrapolate, namely process-based models, monitoring networks, remote sensing, and integrated economic frameworks. \textcite{Ma2025} distil this program broadly, arguing that more research is needed to comprehensively understand the impacts of conservation practices on agricultural productivity, nutrient-loss reduction, ecosystem services, and their tradeoffs in tile-drained agricultural ecosystems. The strongest recurring lines of evidence pointing forward are: (i) the geographic and pedoclimatic narrowness of existing field trials --- concentrated in the U.S. Midwest --- which limits transferability \parencite{Zhao2016,Birru2023}; (ii) persistent structural weaknesses in the crop, cover-crop, drainage, and nutrient modules of biophysical models \parencite{Dietzel2016,Chatterjee2025,Feyereisen2006}; (iii) the need for long-term, multi-season datasets to resolve slow soil-health and climate-interaction signals \parencite{Kaspar2012,Bawa2023,Saha2024}; and (iv) the still-immature integration of biophysical, economic, and policy dimensions needed to guide adoption **[CITATION CHECKED: Ferin2023]**. This section synthesizes these open questions and research priorities rather than settled results.

section: Future Research Needs for Crop-Drainage Systems
subsection: Broadening the empirical base: sites, soils, climates, and long-term observation
claim_paragraph: The call for \emph{long-term} experimentation is equally strong. **[CITATION CHECKED: Kaspar2012]** identify a need for additional long-term studies of the effectiveness of winter cover crops over time, and \textcite{Bawa2023} argue that a longer-term study is needed to observe the positive influence of a rye cover crop on soil-health parameters. \textcite{MartinezFeria2016} seek understanding of the long-term consequences of including rye cover crops in Midwestern systems and of the biotic and abiotic mechanisms by which rye affects yield and environmental performance. \textcite{Kumar2014b} note that long-term monitoring of fluxes under different crop rotations is needed because of seasonal climatic fluctuations. Several teams describe active or planned long-term programs: \textcite{Qi2025b} report ongoing rice--wheat and rice--oil rotation experiments to further assess subsurface-drainage performance over multiple seasons and climates; \textcite{Liu2025b} and \textcite{Liu2025c} call for long-term monitoring of subsurface pipe drainage and seepage-drainage effects across diverse environmental conditions and cropping systems; and \textcite{Thoma2005} caution that four years of data are insufficient to resolve whether higher residue cover minimizes pollutant losses and affects grain yield over time. \textcite{Acharya2019b} similarly call for a more detailed and longer-term experiment to understand climate--crop-management interactions.

section: Future Research Needs for Crop-Drainage Systems
subsection: Advancing process-based and biophysical models
claim_paragraph: Beyond cover-crop and drainage modules, authors call broadly for stronger, better-validated, and more transferable models. \textcite{SKAGGS1994} state that much remains to be learned about the mechanisms governing pollutant losses from drained soils, that research must improve process understanding before quantification is possible, that methods are needed to quantify how alternative designs and operations affect crop yields and environmental impacts while considering interdependent cultural, fertility, and pest-management practices, and that better datasets are needed to test models across wide ranges of soil, crop, and climate. \textcite{Negm2014} call for more intense field measurements to validate their model and additional testing across conditions, noting its potential for simulating long-term climate-change impacts. \textcite{Grewal2025} prioritize improving prediction of high-load peak events, refining the concentration component of the model, further testing the fertilizer-effect hypothesis under ponding, and empirical data to validate predictions for cover-crop and controlled-drainage practices. \textcite{Gunn2018} report that DRAINMOD is being coupled with a crop model (DSSAT) to capture other factors influencing maize relative yield under subirrigation. \textcite{Tian2012} call for field verification of soil-physical-property changes, investigation of early-successional plant growth and its hydrological effects, verification of temporal stomatal-conductance changes against field measurements, and cautious evaluation of adding understory-growth and prescribed-burning modules. \textcite{Morrison2014} seek greater sensitivity to low flows, yearly crop-information inputs for calibration/validation consistency, and a macropore-flow algorithm to capture poorly draining soils. \textcite{Smith2008} argue that a validated process-based rather than empirical model should be applied to capture complex variable interactions. \textcite{Ndulue2024} recommend incorporating CO\textsubscript{2} effects, diseases, nutrient availability, cultivar type, and planting date for greater confidence in climate-change results. \textcite{Ma2025} argue that systematic data collection on water fluxes, solute-nutrient fluxes, greenhouse-gas emissions, root development, and aboveground biomass would facilitate model validation and refine mechanisms and parameterization. **[CITATION CHECKED: Li2025]** note that winter-crop-growth simulations need additional crop-genetic-parameter calibration and must account for elevated CO\textsubscript{2} and alternative management, and that simpler, faster biophysical models may be viable for large-scale winter-cropland simulation. \textcite{Dietzel2016} additionally call for improved subsurface-drainage simulation within soybean in APSIM. \textcite{Qi2010b} report a field-scale experiment being conducted in parallel to a non-weighing lysimeter study to validate rye cover-crop effects on soil-water dynamics and nitrate leaching, and \textcite{Malone2007c} note that per-plot soil-parameter calibration would improve drainage predictions.

section: Future Research Needs for Crop-Drainage Systems
subsection: Drainage system design, water-table management, and materials
claim_paragraph: Optimizing drainage design for the joint goals of crop yield and water quality is a persistent open problem. \textcite{Kladivko2021} argue that more field studies coupled with modeling are needed to develop site-specific recommendations and to optimize drainage design for both crop yield and water-quality purposes, calling continued efforts on systems approaches "urgently needed." \textcite{Zhao2016} suggest research into alternative drainage spacing aimed at balancing crop production against decreased drainage losses. **[CITATION CHECKED: Singh2007b]** recommend field experiments in Iowa and the Upper Midwest to characterize how shallow and controlled drainage affect the complete water balance and crop production, including potential water-movement pathways, and note that a flexible scheme managing the control structure by soil-moisture status might reduce controlled-drainage impacts on relative yields and surface runoff. \textcite{Nash2015} state that more research is needed to determine whether managed drainage can consistently produce greater corn yield than free drainage, with benefits on claypan soils perhaps concentrated in higher-yield-potential years. \textcite{Nelson2011} call for further evaluation of drainage water management effects on high-yielding soybean cultivars, insect and disease management, cost-effectiveness in corn--soybean rotations, and grain-quality differences on claypan soils. \textcite{Dinnes2002} prioritize low-cost drainage-control and water-table-management designs that can be retrofitted to existing tile lines, and research on wetlands, buffers, and bioreactors to address residence time, carbon sources, land area, and cost limitations.

section: Future Research Needs for Crop-Drainage Systems
subsection: Cover crops: agronomic, environmental, and modeling frontiers
claim_paragraph: Cover-crop \emph{modeling} is a distinct frontier. \textcite{Feyereisen2006} enumerate needed advances: additional validation of the rye growth model, field verification of climate and soil-fertility effects on the ratio of rye N uptake to biomass, adjustment of radiation-use efficiency for atmospheric conditions, and better algorithms for plant N uptake. \textcite{Malone2007c} note that determining correct parameter values for winter cover crops requires thorough testing with several years of field-specific data, and that a more realistic N-uptake routine may improve corn-yield predictions. \textcite{Malone2014b} state that modeling germination and establishment of winter rye needs further research and that further analysis is the next step to assess regional cover-crop impacts. \textcite{Chatterjee2025} report that calibration of soil-organic-matter and drained-upper-limit parameters is critical and that a dedicated crop module for simulating winter rye could improve prediction of aboveground biomass and its consequences for cash-crop yield and water and N flux. \textcite{Dietzel2016} identify weaknesses in APSIM related to cover-crop effects on following-corn yields, winter soil temperatures under frozen conditions, and subsurface drainage in soybeans during flooding. \textcite{Gupta2022} propose developing a chemical-termination routine to enhance cover-crop impact studies, and \textcite{Gupta2023b} call for improving the drainage and soil-N mineralization/immobilization modules and studying extreme-event effects on cover-crop impacts to plan field-scale adaptive strategies. **[CITATION CHECKED: Strock2004]** report research in progress to predict cover-crop establishment and growth in Minnesota. \textcite{Singh2023} suggest investigating additional cover crops such as radish and legumes in hydrology and water-quality simulations.

section: Model Validation Across Diverse Conditions
subsection: Field Data and Process Measurements Still Needed
claim_paragraph: Phosphorus transfer is similarly data-limited. Many factors in phosphorus indices require further investigation for their effect on field-to-stream transfer, and a central challenge is to demonstrate that index-based field rankings actually reflect the risk of transfer to open streams **[CITATION CHECKED: Bechmann2007]**. A risk-class approach relying on a multiple-factor index, supported by a large dataset, is advanced as a more reliable predictor of phosphorus leaching \parencite{Beauchemin2003}. Confirming suggested trends in phosphorus movement is argued to require quantitative measurement of preferential flow using tracers \parencite{Salazar2011}, and higher temporal sampling resolution or tracer studies are more generally needed to prove preferential flow and to expose the processes behind observed concentration patterns \parencite{Tiemeyer2009}. Structural model deficiencies around surface runoff generation, surface phosphorus loading, and phosphorus transport in tiles are identified as priorities for more accurate field-scale representation \parencite{Apostel2021}. Where accurate phosphorus transport dynamics are required, automated samplers or real-time sensors are considered necessary \parencite{Dialameh2022}, and sediment behaviour along drainage ditches is proposed as a target for future measurement, aided by high-resolution topographic survey before and after major storms \parencite{Warsta2014}.

section: Model Validation Across Diverse Conditions
subsection: Broadening the Empirical Basis: Sites, Soils, Scales, and Time
claim_paragraph: Extending validation across the climatic and management envelope is a related priority. Models developed under humid conditions are singled out for testing under semi-arid or arid regimes, and for improved simulation of rainfall events following prolonged dry spells \parencite{Prasher1996}. Longer monitoring records are repeatedly invoked as the route to firmer conclusions: continued field measurement over ``a much longer period of time'' is needed to evaluate drainage envelope materials such as rice husk \parencite{Ebrahimian2011}, and more detailed data over longer periods might have altered both system response and apparent model performance \parencite{Negm2017}. Continued field monitoring and modelling are also cited as the means to validate reported results **[CITATION CHECKED: Grazhdani1996]**, while field verification is recommended before analytical tools are used for design or planning \parencite{Hornbuckle2012}. Design-geometry questions add a further dimension, with calls to explore drain spacings wider than 30~m through additional experiments \parencite{Mathew2001} and to answer regionally how much drainage efficiency loss to expect and which design rainstorm to adopt \parencite{Wiskow2003}. Finally, several authors stress that combinations of measures and models must be adapted and optimised to local field conditions rather than assumed portable \parencite{MULLER1988}, and that field studies remain necessary simply to confirm that simulations hold \parencite{Shipitalo2016,Yousfi2014}.

section: Model Validation Across Diverse Conditions
subsection: Calibration, Sensitivity Analysis, and Uncertainty
claim_paragraph: Automated and global approaches to calibration and sensitivity analysis are widely advocated. Automatic calibration methods are called for to support robust parameter sensitivity analysis, with ensemble Kalman filtering identified as a promising option for parameter identification \parencite{Warsta2014}, and autocalibration of parameters is recommended alongside algorithms to accelerate solution of the Richards equation \parencite{Sadhukhan2019b}. Automatic calibration is noted as an increasingly suggested practice generally \parencite{Singh2019b}. Global sensitivity analysis is proposed to capture parameter interactions not resolved by local one-at-a-time methods such as LH-OAT \parencite{Timalsina2023}, sensitivity analysis is recommended to understand parameter influence on model performance in depth \parencite{Chelil2022}, and model sensitivity to all parameters is urged to be analysed under several flow conditions \parencite{Kacimov2000}. For revised SWAT, further studies are needed to establish suitable lower and upper bounds of the sensitivity adjustment factor, with additional work underway on winter and growing-season water and nitrogen budgets **[CITATION CHECKED: Moriasi2013b]**. At catchment scale, spatially distributed streambed conductance is proposed for reach-level calibration, and groundwater--surface-water exchange fluxes are suggested as additional calibration targets to constrain models and as a possible proxy for the drainage contribution to streamflow \parencite{Karan2021}.

section: Model Validation Across Diverse Conditions
subsection: Instrumentation and Measurement-Method Validation
claim_paragraph: Emerging measurement technologies carry explicit validation requirements before field deployment. A computer-vision flow-measurement approach requires more data to verify robustness in real-world environments and testing under more variable conditions, with model modifications---such as incorporating the Manning--Strickler equation to compensate for uneven horizontal initial velocities---and attention to data storage, transmission, and reduction for long-term deployment \parencite{Young2023}. For high-precision topographic survey under less-than-ideal real-time-kinematic conditions, hybrid RTK--rotating-laser systems or interpolated total-station surfaces are offered as alternatives \parencite{Freeland2014}. Sensor and device design is also flagged for refinement, including adaptation of a basic design for other target ranges and improvement of the coefficient of variation for mass-produced units \parencite{Enamorado2007}, and examination of the humidity-stability effect on sensible-heat-flux estimates from large-aperture scintillometry \parencite{Zhang2010}. Hydraulic-loss measurement remains incomplete: further work is needed on head loss in corrugated-pipe junctions and manholes under free-surface flow, with the possibility of discharge-specific head-loss coefficient relationships noted \parencite{Bayat2011}; on friction energy loss, flow velocities, detailed free-surface elevations, and transitional cavity-flow conditions **[CITATION CHECKED: Nédélec2008]**; on the influence of declining-bend slope on air discharge across several distortion heights \parencite{Gurklys2008}; and on modifying existing formulae to apply an appropriate Manning coefficient for design \parencite{Kouchakzadeh2011}. Strain-gauge experiments are identified as necessary to generate input data characterising the non-linear behaviour of single-wall corrugated HDPE pipe \parencite{Gaj2021}.

section: Model Validation Across Diverse Conditions
subsection: Model Structure, Coupling, and Learning Approaches
claim_paragraph: Refinements to the physical and analytical basis of drainage models are also proposed. Numerical models incorporating aquifer homogeneity, anisotropy, and varying bottom slopes are envisioned, with existing analytical solutions serving to verify them \parencite{Lin2025}; conversely, results from simple models are recommended for cross-checking against more general models and vice versa, collating several analytical approaches, running numerical codes such as MODFLOW, and verifying in the field \parencite{Kacimov2000}. Reanalysis using the Laplace rather than the Boussinesq equation, and extension of in-situ validation to slow-response systems, are proposed \parencite{Bouarfa2000}, while comparison of semi-analytical, fully numerical, and extended analytical solutions is reported as ongoing \parencite{Wiskow2003}. Recession-based equations are proposed for extension to spatially varying soil properties by replacing constant hydraulic conductivity and drainable porosity with functions of distance from the drain, with the effect of slope requiring further work \parencite{Cooke2001}. A three-dimensional flow model is suggested as potentially more suitable at a heterogeneous field site, with independent mathematical treatment and more controlled laboratory and field experiments warranted to make similar-media scaling approaches more robust \parencite{Mohanty1997}. Solute mixing is proposed to be represented with distinct mixing-layer depths and partition coefficients for mixing and outflow stages, the exact nature of the process remaining to be investigated **[CITATION CHECKED: Shalit1996]**. Additional targeted refinements include reconsidering the assumption of constant deep percolation and the treatment of shallow water tables persisting within 0.3~m of the surface \parencite{Kolars2019}, further study of spacing and depth through experiment and steady-state analytic--numerical simulation \parencite{Saptomo2021}, and concurrent comparison of outflow and water-table recessions observed at a single site \parencite{VANDELEUR1959}. Strengthening index-system construction and the evaluation of calculation reliability, supported by more samples and additional indicators such as soil thickness, grain size, composition, density, effective porosity, and permeability, is urged to enable deeper mechanistic development \parencite{Hou2018}, and building a dedicated simulation model to extend experimental findings is likewise planned \parencite{Tao2019b}.

section: Bioreactor Design and Research Gaps
subsection: Phosphorus-removal media and filter design
claim_paragraph: Fly-ash and pellet media raise saturation-timing questions. \textcite{Li2017} stress that saturation time must be quantified before field application so that fly-ash pellets can be replaced before they shift from phosphorus sink to source, and \textcite{Li2018b} direct follow-up research toward the hydraulic parameters of fly-ash pellets combined with recovery, and toward constraints such as poor saturation time, high outflow pH, and possible field desorption. Filter-media blends more broadly remain unoptimised: **[CITATION CHECKED: Agrawal2011]** call for determining the feasibility of filter installation and long-term field-scale performance, and \textcite{Agrawal2011b} report a need to determine the optimal media blend and configuration, to identify which constituent(s) offload phosphate and for how long before saturation, and to design larger or new filters capable of accommodating high drainage flows with sufficient contact time. Contact-time resolution itself is flagged by \textcite{Kumari2025}, who suggest exploring shorter contact-time intervals (e.g., 30~min) to capture the rapid initial adsorption phase. Anisotropic-medium behaviour warrants further study per \textcite{Kankarej2023}. Integrated woodchip-plus-PSM designs need multi-scale evaluation: \textcite{Husk2018} call for assessing mixed-media phosphorus-removal effectiveness under additional climate, soil, and cropping conditions over multiyear periods and at different scales to develop predictive design models, evaluating alternative or multiple media placements within bioreactors, examining effective P-removal lifespan and reuse/regeneration/recycling potential, and studying operational parameters such as pH, biochemical oxygen demand, and conductivity, including microbially mediated processes and removal of agrochemicals and microbial contaminants.

section: Bioreactor Design and Research Gaps
subsection: Contaminant transport through drainage inlets and macropores
claim_paragraph: Understanding how contaminants enter and move through drainage networks is explicitly under-studied. \textcite{Li2017b} recommend additional research on how nitrate, phosphorus, and pesticides are transported through drainage inlets, studies of inlet performance under different debris from different crop systems, and modification of the flow equations to represent actual inlet performance under debris conditions. The definition of a bioreactor's effective contributing area is itself uncertain; \textcite{Akay2008} question whether the contributing area should vary for water, tracers, and reactive contaminants. Sediment behaviour within tiles is likewise unresolved: **[CITATION CHECKED: Stone1997]** note that the relative importance of bacteria versus solution-chemistry changes on flocculation of tile sediment across a range of turbulent shear stresses remains to be determined.

section: Data and Experimental Validation Needs
subsection: Overview
claim_paragraph: A recurring conclusion across the tile-drainage literature is that theory, models, and management hypotheses have outrun the field data available to validate them. The studies surveyed here converge on a shared research frontier defined less by a lack of ideas than by a lack of evidence: process representations that remain untested outside the conditions in which they were built, models whose parameters cannot be constrained without measurements that were never made, and management practices whose benefits are asserted from short records at single sites. This section synthesises the identified data and experimental-validation needs. Several broad lines of evidence emerge. First, process-based drainage and water-quality models (DRAINMOD and its derivatives, SWAT, APEX, HYDRUS, CRHM, and numerous salinity codes) are repeatedly flagged as requiring further testing across soils, climates, crops, and management systems, with particular weaknesses in phosphorus, macropore/preferential-flow, and seepage components **[CITATION CHECKED: Askar2025]**. Second, there is a strong and near-universal call for long-term, year-round, and multi-site monitoring to close water and nutrient budgets \parencite{Kladivko2001,Sharpley2019,Frankenberger2024}. Third, rapidly maturing remote-sensing and geophysical methods for mapping drainage networks need systematic evaluation of the site conditions under which they succeed \parencite{Carlsen2024,Wienken2024}. Fourth, emerging management strategies -- controlled drainage, drainage water recycling, and edge-of-field treatment -- lack the coordinated field-scale experiments and simulations needed to quantify their trade-offs \parencite{Hay2021,Youssef2018,Mendes2020}. Finally, authors repeatedly emphasise improvements to experimental design, statistical methodology, uncertainty quantification, and the reporting of site characterisation, management, and economic data \parencite{Pagliari2021,Singh2022b,Gates2002}. The subsections below organise these needs by domain.

section: Data and Experimental Validation Needs
subsection: Economic feasibility, management data, and databases
claim_paragraph: A final cluster of needs concerns the socio-economic and data-infrastructure context of drainage research. Economic feasibility analyses are repeatedly requested: cost-benefit analysis of surface amendments and energy savings \parencite{Wamono2016b}, regional economic benefits of drainage water recycling under future climate and droughts with optimised reservoir dimensions \parencite{Kosari2024}, overall economic benefit and inter-BMP interactions of integrated systems \parencite{Li2021b}, comprehensive cost-benefit analysis of subsurface drainage accounting for short- and long-term effects \parencite{Guo2025}, economic feasibility of drainage as a preventive measure against salinisation \parencite{Datta2000,HalbacCotoaraZamfir2022}, cost and consumption in paddy fields \parencite{Jia2023}, cost-efficiency of edge-of-field technologies \parencite{Mendes2020}, and cost reduction and technology sophistication \parencite{Okuda2020}. Detailed management and soil data are emphasised as prerequisites for reliable inference: verification of soil information by field sampling and farmer records with accurate management data \parencite{JORJANI1991}, detailed agricultural-management information and soil-carbon change as watershed-study priorities \parencite{Williams2017}, sound pedological and geological knowledge for interpreting drainage concentrations \parencite{Jacobsen2007}, and richer site characterisation and variability reporting \parencite{Singh2022b}. Data-infrastructure and regionalisation needs are prominent in the German mapping work of \textcite{Hirt2005,Hirt2005b,Hirt2011}, which calls for comprehensive databases of tile-drained land proportions by soil type, validation of existing databases, extrapolation from eastern to western Germany and to European soil maps at the mesoscale, and inclusion of drained areas in water- and nutrient-flux models so that mitigation measures can be designed; the approach is transferable where representative drainage data and medium-scale soil maps exist. Coordinated, coupled field-and-simulation research programmes are called for to advance drainage water recycling across hydrology, crop-yield, water-quality, complementary, and implementation categories, with monitoring across sites and climates to document downstream load reductions and reservoir behaviour \parencite{Hay2021}, alongside soil-moisture-sensor and remote monitoring of control structures, validation under increasing climate variability, and additional well-characterised sites \parencite{Willison2021}. Continued monitoring of salinity and multi-scale water quality is essential to refine drainage-reuse strategy \parencite{ElAgha2020}, and forestry, land-use, and topographic effects on runoff generation and nitrogen retention require further analysis in Nordic and Baltic settings **[CITATION CHECKED: Deelstra2014b]**. Site-specific reservoir and constructed-wetland sizing \parencite{Haverstock2017}, coupling of soil-water simulation with management-scenario testing \parencite{Bulot2017}, verification of sulphur-loss and other process models under a range of climatic, management, and soil conditions \parencite{SMITH1983}, and evaluation of forest water-management systems and best management practices \parencite{MCCARTHY1992} round out the distributed set of data and validation needs that define this research frontier.

section: Data and Experimental Validation Needs
subsection: Experimental design, statistics, and uncertainty quantification
claim_paragraph: Several authors identify methodological rather than substantive gaps. \textcite{Pagliari2021} call for confirming whether beta distributions or time series are the best approaches for analysing field-scale, unreplicated paired drainage experiments, or whether new statistical methodologies are needed for controlled-drainage studies. \textcite{Andrus2014} argue that directed investigations of specific hypotheses are more productive than replicate spatial analyses of additional biofilters and recommend more frequent shallow sampling at specified spacings. \textcite{Okuda2020} note that field experiments with replication are needed to enable statistical analysis, and \textcite{Wamono2016b} recommend matching tractor power to implement size, comparing on a percentage basis, and adding measurements of draft, slip, and trafficability. Uncertainty quantification recurs strongly: stochastic and sensitivity analyses to address parametric uncertainty **[CITATION CHECKED: Gates2002]**, robust/stochastic optimisation for parameter and input uncertainty \parencite{Lei2026}, explicit estimation of prediction accuracy and uncertainty in phosphorus models \parencite{Radcliffe2015}, reduction of interpreter-based mapping uncertainty \parencite{Redoloza2023}, and analysis of the hydrological model's contribution to total uncertainty using multiple models \parencite{Jeantet2022}. Improved sampling and measurement designs are recommended for buffer and riparian studies, including more sampling wells to capture spatial variability, tracer studies to attribute flow proportions, and both surface and dissolved N$_2$O measurements \parencite{Davis2019}, and dye tracing, control wells, and paired free-flowing watershed comparisons at saturated-buffer sites \parencite{Jacquemin2020}. Improved model performance is also sought through better evapotranspiration estimation and additional predictor variables \parencite{Morrison2013}, additional SWAT performance metrics, parameter refinement, longer observation periods, and larger datasets \parencite{Zheng2025b}, and independent evaluation of calibrated models against withheld data \parencite{Schoups2005}. \textcite{Schoups2005} further suggest spatially distributing parameters to remove trade-offs between shallow and deep water tables and multi-objective optimisation with additional criteria.

section: Data and Experimental Validation Needs
subsection: Remote sensing and geophysical mapping of drainage networks
claim_paragraph: Detecting and mapping buried drainage systems is a fast-moving frontier where methods work in some conditions but lack systematic guidelines. \textcite{Wienken2024} describe a functioning non-invasive detection method as indispensable, call for urgent development of holistic and efficient methodologies for aging drainage systems, and recommend combining UAV flights with ground-penetrating radar (GPR) for improved mapping and characterisation. \textcite{Allred2020} lay out an extensive UAV agenda: additional visible, multispectral, and thermal-infrared surveys at multiple farm sites visited repeatedly over two years to define the range of site conditions under which each imagery type maps drain lines; soil temperature and emissivity measurements in small test plots of variable soil, wetness, and cover; advanced processing (band stacking with decorrelation stretch, minimum-noise-fraction and principal-component transforms); supervised machine-learning algorithms to distinguish drain-line responses from field-operation features; and decision-tree guidelines for practitioners. Related UAV/thermal work seeks site-condition guidelines, test-plot quantification of surface thermal behaviour, advanced image processing, and machine learning to differentiate responses \parencite{Allred2021}, and extends thermal-infrared methods to drainage-outlet detection under Midwestern conditions while assessing the hydrologic impacts of outlets on ditches and streams \parencite{Allred2022}. \textcite{Carlsen2024} recommend reconsidering the often-cited 2.54~cm minimum rainfall for imagery acquisition, investigating deep learning and multitemporal acquisition for drained-area segmentation and tile detection, exploring synthetic aperture radar, determining the spatial resolution necessary for tile delineation, performing more large-scale deep-learning studies, bridging computer-science and geoscience practices through uniform evaluation standards, and expanding publicly available drainage-map datasets. Machine-learning mapping across regions is further advanced by calls for deep-learning and transformer-based encoder-decoder architectures, higher-resolution imagery (harmonised Landsat/Sentinel-2, Planet, or aerial), broader spatial and temporal application, and integration into hydrologic and water-quality modelling frameworks \parencite{Wan2024}, and by reducing tracing uncertainty through multiple interpreters, ground-truthed datasets, additional raster covariates (soil type, surface cover, time of year), wind-turbine training examples, and satellite time series \parencite{Redoloza2023}. Geophysical evaluations echo these needs: near-surface geophysical data from more sites and diverse soils \parencite{Allred2005}; systematic testing of antenna configuration, frequency, and antenna-to-pipe orientation across soil types for GPR \parencite{Allred2013}; prediction of GPR suitability via electromagnetic simulation (e.g., gprMax) from EMI measurements and understanding dependence on soil type, residue, tillage, ground wetness, and prior rainfall \parencite{Koganti2020,Koganti2021}; concurrent EMI/GPR and complementary drone-imagery and magnetic-gradiometer surveys \parencite{Koganti2020}; and resistivity/electromagnetic tracer approaches designed for slope and known drain orientation \parencite{Jouen2018}. Optical, radar, and topographic covariate studies also seek more frequent imaging \parencite{Tlapáková2017}, repeated SAR acquisitions with ground-based measurements to track crop growth across drainage ridges \parencite{Meunier2001}, UAV-based cover-crop biomass and N-uptake mapping across landscapes \parencite{Xu2018}, and richer topographic and soil covariates in statistical drainage models **[CITATION CHECKED: Harris2018]**.

section: Data and Experimental Validation Needs
subsection: Validation and improvement of process-based drainage models
claim_paragraph: A cross-cutting structural gap is the representation of seepage, groundwater exchange, and preferential flow. \textcite{DaneshYazdi2016} suggest that groundwater contributions could be incorporated through a double-storage model and residual storage added if hydrochemical data were available, requiring further data to refine interpretations. \textcite{Feng2018} argue that lateral seepage must be allowed to vary during simulation and be included among model inputs, and **[CITATION CHECKED: Kelleners2000]** echo the difficulty of representing regional seepage. \textcite{Kompanizare2024} recommend adapting new tile-drainage modules to different soil textures such as clay loam where preferential flow strongly affects saturated storage and tile flow, adding explicit unsaturated-flow representation where groundwater is disconnected from surface water, integrating with frozen-soil and water-quality modules, and expanding to larger areas. \textcite{Reid2012} stress that more work is needed to quantify the range of macropore flows to tile drains across soil types and management systems, that seasonal (growing versus non-growing) hydrologic regimes should be treated as discrete, and that a framework is offered to encourage others to gather suitable data for testing. \textcite{Allaire2011} call for testing each preferential-flow component individually, validating them in the field, and analysing the individual impact of each component on water quality, including extreme values. \textcite{Ojeda2018} require a more accurate, independent method for determining daily subsurface drainage from one layer to the next given preferential flow, plus sensitivity analysis to identify key parameters needing measurement. \textcite{Ulén2016} note that quantification of macropore flow paths is necessary for proper understanding of subsurface-drain leaching losses and that a dynamic model accounting for frozen soil and air temperature, together with measured data on soil structure and soil-P, is urgently needed. \textcite{Frey2012} call for characterising near-surface preferential flow paths across different soil, land-use, and climatic settings, and \textcite{LESAFFRE1988} note that a better understanding of by-pass flow through cracks is necessary to extend model application to full-year operation, alongside continued field experimentation and automatic calibration of water-table shape coefficients. Nitrogen-cycle and hydrological process representations attract parallel needs: \textcite{Malone2017} suggest developing a surface-residue component, a more detailed drainage approach, more thorough investigation of soil field capacity for denitrification and N losses, and mobile/immobile water phases to improve nitrate transport; \textcite{Gillette2018} call for more empirical data on interactions between soil-water retention and the soil-N budget, including mineralisation and denitrification, and for well-tested models and the use of soft data and complete N budgets during calibration. Analytical and theoretical advances -- rigorous theoretical analysis, formulas for sloped and multilayer soils, and field examination -- are sought for improved subsurface-drainage designs \parencite{Tao2016,Tao2019}, and time-step selection is flagged as a study-specific choice requiring pre-assessment \parencite{Awad2022b}. Other process needs include temporal variability in decay coefficients and deterministic approaches for land-use effects on tile-drained water quality \parencite{Rudra2005}, improved transient and inversely calibrated representations \parencite{Sedaghatdoost2018}, and machine-learning surrogate models that expand training datasets across diverse climatic and hydrogeological conditions, incorporate transient processes and robust/stochastic optimisation, and integrate with real-time control \parencite{Lei2026}.

section: Data and Experimental Validation Needs
subsection: Transferability across soils, climates, crops, and management
claim_paragraph: A pervasive limitation is that findings from single sites or narrow conditions cannot yet be generalised. \textcite{Singh2022b} recommend that controlled-drainage/subirrigation studies be conducted outside the U.S. Midwest and Canada across diverse climates, crops, and soils; that additional studies compare irrigation methods in terms of water supply and water-balance components; and that site characterisation -- including field slope, soil particle-size distribution by horizon, hydraulic conductivity, drainage class, and soil moisture -- be reported, together with measures of variability. \textcite{Bilotta2008} stress that work must be repeated at larger scales and on different soil types as key modulating factors, and \textcite{Goeken2015} call for investigations across geographic regions, diverse perennial species and mixtures, and varied precipitation and weather. \textcite{Nuutinen2001} recommend repeating earthworm-drainage studies on soils of different texture and under less rainy conditions and including other earthworm species, while \textcite{Nuutinen2011} seek horizontal-transect observations to strengthen source-area interpretation and long-term relation of colonisation to soil structure and hydrology. Climate-focused transferability needs include high-resolution climate-change scenarios and effects on lodging, erosion, and agrochemical transport \parencite{Rasmussen2018}; analysis of hydrological-model contributions to total uncertainty using multiple models and assessment at additional French sites under different climates and soils \parencite{Jeantet2022}; and validation of drainage-warming and soil-texture effects on crops via further study and modelling \parencite{Jin2008}. Crop- and practice-specific extensions are sought for paddy and trench drainage \parencite{Rahimi2024,Jia2023}, mole-drainage durability over longer periods and rainy seasons \parencite{JHA1995}, controlled-drainage principles suited to local crops and agronomy in new regions \parencite{Sojka2020}, and interactions of crop rotation and tillage on subsurface drainage \parencite{Ojeda2018}. \textcite{Yu2018} call for further field evaluation of a salt-flushing method, comparison with intermittent ponding, sprinkling, and drip irrigation, an analytical solution for generalisation, and tests in complex heterogeneous soils. Assumptions must be re-verified whenever models are transferred to new areas **[CITATION CHECKED: Youssef2006]**, and localised design methods must be developed to reflect local agro-technical conditions \parencite{Tlapáková2017}.

section: Data and Experimental Validation Needs
subsection: Water balance, seepage, and groundwater interactions
claim_paragraph: Closing the water balance -- particularly seepage and groundwater exchange -- remains a persistent data gap. \textcite{Grose2022} call for further exploration to identify the contribution of groundwater relative to other sources during stormflows, and \textcite{DaneshYazdi2016} would incorporate groundwater through double-storage modelling. \textcite{Sedaghatdoost2018} note that providing groundwater-table data in objective functions would help inverse modelling recover soil properties more precisely, and \textcite{Feng2018} advocate incorporating variable lateral seepage. Regional groundwater assessments call for further radiocarbon sampling and continued rigorous evaluation of changing resource origins \parencite{Tweed2018}, monitoring of groundwater chemistry at recharge zones of well-fields for both shallow and deep flow systems \parencite{Dragon2016}, and additional geologic and hydrologic data plus analysis of deep percolation through silts and clays \parencite{BOOKMAN1959}. Aquifer characterisation needs include accurate descriptions of the hydraulic properties of different aquifer layers \parencite{KAMRA1991} and intensive investigation of the impervious-layer depth to assess effluent-salinity variation under alternative drainage designs \parencite{KAMRA1994}. \textcite{Stuetz2004} recommend greater use of test wells to establish hydrochemical conditions and greater attention to water quality and well design to minimise biofouling. \textcite{Schilling2022} suggest transient simulations to test steady-state assumptions and further research on the capacity of waterways to process excess water, and \textcite{Xu2022} note that updated local groundwater-dynamics information is necessary for siting retention devices. Watershed-scale salt and water studies plan continued data collection with unsteady flow and mass-transport models, sensitivity and stochastic analysis, and consideration of canal lining, horizontal subsurface drainage, and river-level management \parencite{Gates2002,Burkhalter2006}. Groundwater as an alternative water source and the effects of drainage from saline-alkali lands on groundwater are flagged for investigation **[CITATION CHECKED: Zheng2025b]**, as are the interrelation of irrigation practice and drainage design \parencite{Sinai2005} and long-term groundwater-level effects of new drainage \parencite{Okuda2020}. \textcite{Keller2008} suggest that long-term amelioration of nitrogen contamination may require perennial deep-rooted crops and are investigating applicability at larger watershed scales.

section: Subsurface Drainage Flow Modeling Research Gaps
subsection: Climate change, coupled processes, and integrative directions
claim_paragraph: Finally, several authors emphasise that technical advances must be coupled with socio-economic considerations, extension, and demonstration. \textcite{BenAissa2013} advocate a participatory approach to design, testing mixed traditional-ditch and modern-pipe systems and adequate envelopes in situ, and designing systems for easy farmer inspection and maintenance, echoed by \textcite{HajAmor2019} on raising farmer and stakeholder awareness of water and soil management. \textcite{MCFARLANE1992} call for greater extension through demonstrations and documented case studies and for better research on drains' effects on salinity, erosion, structural decline, and phosphate export, and \textcite{Mante2018} note that field managers must weigh the benefit of narrower spacing against impacts on field operations and long-term yield. Cost feasibility is a recurring concern---for changing drainage layout, and \textcite{Imran2021} stresses it specifically for redesigning main drains for free gravity outflow---and \textcite{Malota2015} suggest linking DRAINMOD outputs to a drainage-system cost-minimisation model. \textcite{Lamsodis2011} add operational recommendations, including annual drain-mouth cleaning and managed control of beaver populations, while \textcite{DarziNaftchali2017} argue that surface- and groundwater susceptibility to nitrogen losses should be a major criterion in drain depth and spacing design and that measures are needed at first planting after installation. \textcite{HARRIS1993} note that an increased drainage design standard may be necessary to avoid pipe damage and that direct drilling on sloping undrained land should be avoided, and **[CITATION CHECKED: CAMP1982]** stress ensuring adequate surface and internal drainage for flat-planted sugarcane. Collectively these directions point toward an integrated research agenda in which improved process representation, denser and longer-term data, and explicit economic and management context advance together.

section: Subsurface Drainage Flow Modeling Research Gaps
subsection: Long-term monitoring and revision of design criteria
claim_paragraph: Many site studies conclude that established design criteria require re-evaluation. **[CITATION CHECKED: Christen2001]** call for new drainage design criteria protecting crops while minimising drain-water salinity and volume, reassessment of criteria in light of land-use and irrigation change, and novel saline-water disposal options. \textcite{Muhammad2021} recommend updating criteria and decreasing drain depth to 120~cm at some sites and 100~cm at others while holding spacing constant, and \textcite{Malota2016} call for revisiting design criteria to account for land slope and for recalculating drain spacing (currently 54~m in clay and 74~m in clay-loam soils). \textcite{Bahçeci2009} argue that a lower drain-discharge rate should inform future design in the Harran Plain, while \textcite{Kahlown2002} conclude that subsurface drainage interventions must not go deeper than 2~m and that findings still require field and laboratory confirmation. \textcite{Mante2022} state that the recommended 12--15~m (up to 90~m) spacing for sandy loams must be reviewed and paired with controlled-traffic farming at narrower spacing ($\le$12~m, 0.9~m depth), and \textcite{Nelson2017} call for determining the cost-effectiveness of tile spacings below 6.1~m in claypan soils. \textcite{HajAmor2019} identify a need to design new drainage systems--- including standard guidelines for depth and spacing---and to test them in situ before extension, and \textcite{Skaggs2017} advocate standardising the definition of the drainage coefficient and the consistent use of the Kirkham coefficient and drainage intensity to enable comparison across studies. \textcite{GALLICHAND1992b} suggest implementing design procedures within CAD/GIS-based drainage-design software.

section: Subsurface Drainage Flow Modeling Research Gaps
subsection: Controlled drainage, drainage water management, and novel structures
claim_paragraph: Optimal layout and burial-depth determination in saline and problem soils recur in recent Chinese studies. \textcite{Tian2023} stress considering the appropriate ditching depth when determining optimal pipe-layout parameters and selecting it according to actual soil conditions, and \textcite{Tian2024} recommend burying the pipe as far above the restrictive/critical layer as possible when shallow, breaking a shallow restrictive layer by deep ploughing, and combining methods to enhance drainage. \textcite{Tian2023c} identify layout-parameter selection as the next research target and suggest amendments such as organic fertiliser, straw biochar, or low-permeability mulch film, and \textcite{Zhang2024d} call for adding factors such as buried-pipe depth and fertiliser ratios to improve the saline-soil improvement system. \textcite{Zhai2023} advocate optimising hidden-pipe layout through a multi-scheme decision model and distinguishing nitrous-oxide-emission sources, and **[CITATION CHECKED: Han2023]** plan to include construction cost when clarifying the appropriate range of buried depths. \textcite{Qian2025b} recommend improving the design drainage objective when using models to set pipe parameters, \textcite{Ren2021} call for studying combination forms under different rainfall and unsaturated initial conditions using mathematical models of economic factors, and \textcite{Zheng2025} propose field experiments on the interaction between drain spacing and outlet height to develop water- and salt-regulation control strategies. \textcite{SerranoCoronel2018} state that water-movement behaviour under different configurations must be studied, and \textcite{Zegeye2021} suggest modifying drain depth and spacing using better soil-permeability information and integrating bank dewatering with other gully rehabilitation measures.

section: Subsurface Drainage Flow Modeling Research Gaps
subsection: Preferential and macropore flow: characterisation and modelling
claim_paragraph: Improvements to macropore process descriptions are proposed across several model frameworks. \textcite{Li2023d} call for further study of preferential flow in macropore channels and appropriate modification of the RZWQM2 macropore component---better partitioning of soil water between matrix and macropore flow, improved macropore channel flow to shorten the drainage-peak recession time, and calibration of macropore parameters against sub-hourly drainage data. At watershed scale, **[CITATION CHECKED: Poon2021]** suggest adjusting the percolation algorithm to account for dynamic macropore connectivity or effective macroporosity and to include a soil-moisture factor describing matrix--macropore water transfer during the growing season, noting that experimental measurements of soil macroporosity and site-specific measurements of major soil types and management practices are needed to select appropriate connectivity values. \textcite{Villholth1998b} propose including small-scale diffusion across the micropore space or adding more domains to the model description, while cautioning that such remedies demand more elaborate models and more parameters, and stress the importance of site-specific measurements of matrix and macropore hydraulic conductivity. \textcite{Villholth1998} further note that the dynamics of macropore structure at the soil surface and their influence on chemical transport deserve additional study, and that whether vertical macropore transport occurs in deeper saturated layers--- especially in areas dominated by regional groundwater recharge---remains to be investigated.

section: Subsurface Drainage Flow Modeling Research Gaps
subsection: Calibration, validation, parameterisation, and data needs
claim_paragraph: Beyond the properties themselves, authors emphasise improved calibration strategy and the acquisition of complementary observations. \textcite{Boico2022} recommend calibration with parameter-estimation software to overcome poor representation of soil hydraulic properties and the implementation of multiple conceptual models to represent plausible heterogeneity structures. \textcite{Schneider2022} propose a more flexible parameterisation for drain-sensitive parameters such as the conductivity of the uppermost geologic layers, a fully distributed conductivity field with pilot-point calibration, additional observation types such as soil moisture to reduce overparameterisation, finer horizontal and vertical resolutions with a more complex unsaturated-zone description and explicit drain representation, and integration of proxy datasets such as machine-learning predictions of drain probability or average drain flow with physically based models. \textcite{DeSchepper2017} suggest combining catchment- and drainage-discharge calibration, and **[CITATION CHECKED: Sedaghatdoost2019]** recommend using drainage salinity data alongside other measured data in the objective function. \textcite{Brighenti2023} propose testing alternative objective functions such as the Kling--Gupta efficiency and establishing relationships between plot-scale measured tile flow and watershed-scale calculated tile flow.

section: Reducing Nitrate Losses via Management
subsection: Fertilizer nitrogen management: rate, timing, form, and crediting
claim_paragraph: \subsubsection{Enhanced-efficiency fertilizers, stabilizers, and application method} Beyond rate and timing, several authors point to product- and method-level questions. \textcite{Kaur2024c} recommend that future research address enhanced-efficiency fertilizer technology---spring-applied anhydrous ammonia with a nitrification inhibitor---in conjunction with enhanced drainage water management in corn--soybean rotations. \textcite{Vincent2025} note that management of NH$_4^+$-N specifically can be achieved through N stabilizers applied alongside fertilizers, and that the effects of cover crops on field- and watershed-scale NH$_4^+$-N dynamics deserve further exploration. Regarding manure delivery, **[CITATION CHECKED: Gamble2018]** report that drainage NO$_3$-N concentrations from fertigated silage corn need further study to determine whether they can be reduced to acceptable levels without impacting silage yield, and stress that tradeoffs of fertigation---crop injury, disease, pathogen transport to waterways, and alternative N-loss pathways relative to slurry injection---require further exploration. \textcite{Bechmann2014} recommend developing a strategy to even out manure application within catchments of high livestock density, and that mitigation in cereal areas should focus on reducing soil mineral N in spring and autumn.

section: Reducing Nitrate Losses via Management
subsection: Process-based modeling: outstanding algorithmic and evaluation gaps
claim_paragraph: \subsubsection{Drain-design decision support and validation} **[CITATION CHECKED: Moriasi2013]** propose using the Revised SWAT model to determine optimum drain depth and spacing that reduce NO$_3$-N losses while optimizing yield, but stress that validation studies of the Hooghoudt and Kirkham tile-drain equations in Revised SWAT are needed before use as a decision-support tool. \textcite{Ale2012} recommend validating a nitrate-load methodology by comparison with N models such as DRAINMOD-NII or RZWQM and by evaluation in additional watersheds where loads from both tile drains and streamflow have been measured. \textcite{Ng2000} note that NO$_3$-N leaching modeling for at least one year is required and that further calibration with consecutive multi-year data may improve prediction for free-drainage treatments. \textcite{Skaggs1995} caution that additional testing for other soils, crops, and locations is needed before routine model application. \textcite{Malone2007} argue that overcoming regression-based limitations and comprehensively quantifying yield and nitrate loading requires process-based models, that simulation results under different conditions could feed a database for economic and risk analysis, and that developing regression equations is a step toward a simple, accurate, objective method to quantify management and climate effects on nitrate loading and yield for a region.

section: Long-Term Monitoring and Research Needs
subsection: The Case for Long-Term, Multi-Year Monitoring
claim_paragraph: At the site scale, numerous studies attach their conclusions to explicit requirements for additional years of observation. **[CITATION CHECKED: Jaynes2008]** state that continued monitoring of the denitrification-wall treatment for additional years is necessary to clearly quantify its effectiveness given natural variability in weather and crop growth, that extended monitoring is required to quantify effectiveness over time, and that further work is needed to determine the long-term cost per unit of nitrate removed and the system's potential as a management tool. \textcite{Dalhem2019} note that continued sampling and measurements will reveal how long the positive effects of the treatments persist. \textcite{Osterholm2005} judge it worthwhile to monitor a test site for several more years to better assess the functionality of a combination of two techniques, while \textcite{ROLLIN1987} plan to gather additional observations covering a longer service-life period. Similar calls come from \textcite{Wesström2015}, who require verification over a longer monitoring period, \textcite{Reinhart2020}, who call for more widespread and longer-duration evaluations to better understand a practice's potential impact, and \textcite{Rijal2012}, who identify a need to assess the replicability of results in time. \textcite{GiménezValero2025} similarly conclude that additional multi-year measurements will be necessary to confirm whether observed differences persist under comparable environmental and management conditions. Underlying all of these is the disciplinary-scale argument of \textcite{SPALING1995} for long-term monitoring of environmental change at various scales.

section: Long-Term Organic Soil Drainage Research Gaps
subsection: Modelling, reactive transport, and specialised soils
claim_paragraph: For reclaimed saline and waterlogged Vertisols, \textcite{Mukhopadhyay2023} and \textcite{Mukhopadhyay2023b} call for studies of how SSD integrated with crop management (inorganic fertilisers, crop residues, compost, green manure) affects soil-quality improvement and carbon-sequestration potential, of N/P/K losses and field-scale budgeting across more sites and larger Vertisol areas, of efficient recycling of drained water, and of greenhouse-gas fluxes before and after SSD installation to assess climate-mitigation potential. \textcite{ElGhannam2023} call for long-term study of controlled drainage's effect on soil salinity and for site-specific salinity-management practices to avoid salinization under long-term shallow groundwater. \textcite{Colombani2016} call for investigation of salt-crust formation and the subsequent transport of dissolved species, detailed soil-physical analysis of long-term tillage, and more sustainable practices (accurate fertiliser scheduling, frequent small irrigations after fertilisation, and buffer zones to abate excess N). \textcite{SoltaniGerdefaramarzi2020} suggest investigating leaching effects on other elements such as plant-available potassium, analysing at least three soil samples at longitudinal distances from the drain and at different depths by combined sampling, and testing organic modifiers such as animal manures to improve leaching efficiency. \textcite{Qian2021} recommend monitoring soil properties such as elemental toxicities in each year of multi-year waterlogging experiments, extending research to different crops and regions, and scheduling field drainage to account for different waterlogging forms, especially during budding, flowering, and boll-forming stages. \textcite{Bahçeci2018} recommend further field research to verify long-term resistance to root growth (especially for perennial crops) and performance under other soil, hydrological, and agricultural conditions, while \textcite{Bahceci2008} note that drainable-porosity ($\mu$) values can be determined in the laboratory, in situ, or by correlation, with more reliable values obtained when soil texture is considered. \textcite{Sadhukhan2019} call for further tests at additional locations under different fertilisation (including manure), soil, climate, and crop conditions over longer periods with more observational data. **[CITATION CHECKED: Isa2023]** call for studies of additive effectiveness (soil strength, rate, cost, impact on rice, physicochemical properties, and soil interaction), land-replacement characterisation and economic evaluation, and integration of rehabilitation methods to maximise soil strength and paddy yield.

section: Long-Term Organic Soil Drainage Research Gaps
subsection: Soil biology, health indicators, and human-induced soil evolution
claim_paragraph: The soil-biology response to changing drainage hydrology is repeatedly flagged as understudied. \textcite{Sherbine2023} call for longer-term evaluation of soil biological indicators to understand how soil biology responds to gradually changing hydrology. \textcite{Yang2025} identify the interaction mechanisms between subsurface drainage (SSD) and soil physicochemical properties, and the response of soil microbial activity, as priorities. \textcite{Kaur2024b} and \textcite{Kumar2014} call for continued research on specific soil microbial properties and microbial community structure and function to explain tillage and drainage impacts. **[CITATION CHECKED: Li2023b]** identify a scalability gap for nematode measurements, recommending DNA-sequencing methods and statistical approaches that quantitatively integrate nematodes with the SHI, and provide a basis for expanding to multiyear assessments of SHI linkages with nutrient losses and crop productivity. \textcite{Nakajima2015} argue that additional long-term studies are needed on the effects of no-till and subsurface drainage on the soil quality index (SQI), that valid, reliable, sensitive, repeatable, and accessible indicators must be identified, and that a framework for overall soil-quality evaluation and a systems approach are needed. \textcite{Singh2007} suggest that soil-enzyme activities could help identify management practices to maintain soil health. \textcite{Masri2024} argue that further research is needed to prove that no-till improves soil-health functions enough to sustainably reduce nitrate leaching, and that an extended research period is needed to relate nitrate load, water-quality parameters, and soil-health functions. \textcite{Caron2025} recommend adding dynamic to static indicators to diagnose compaction (extending to deeper layers and more corn-producing areas) and investigating whether long-term forage rotation or agroforestry can restore soil physical health, including comparative long-term economic viability.

section: Long-Term Organic Soil Drainage Research Gaps
subsection: Phosphorus: better metrics, pathways, and loss prediction
