claim_paragraph: Multiple authors identify the sorption/desorption interface and particulate pathways as poorly resolved. \textcite{Mumbi2025} call for quantifying when and how varying water sources and fluxes interact with soil to desorb and adsorb P---a need considered critical to advancing prediction of subsurface dissolved reactive P (DRP) transport---supported by data across soil types and management (e.g., long-term till vs.\ no-till). \textcite{Flores2021} note the need to understand the mechanisms controlling particulate settling and P desorption. \textcite{Nguyen2002} call for investigating P release--retention characteristics of drainage sediments under prolonged flooding and alternating waterlogged--drying conditions, and the interaction of sediment P with overlying drainage water across flooding, drying, wetting, and P-loading regimes. \textcite{Jiang2010} recommend assessing P fractions after leaching to understand transformations under polyacrylamide (PAM), including its effect on different purple-soil layers and interactions among broadcasting rate, mixing procedure, and leaching losses. \textcite{Wilson2019} highlight the need to quantify the contribution of colloidal P to DRP measurements and to determine whether erosion-mitigating BMPs or nutrient management better control it, alongside clarifying P stratification, preferential flow through tile drainage, and the effectiveness and time-to-effect of subsurface P application in stratified fields. **[CITATION CHECKED: Norgaard2013]** recommend including both dissolved and colloid-associated leaching parameters in field-scale risk assessment, testing a modified Dexter concept using clay and silt as a linking indicator, and considering water-dispersible colloids and tillage events as indicators of particle release.

section: Controlled Drainage and Irrigation Water Management
subsection: Overview
claim_paragraph: Integrating controlled drainage (CD) with irrigation water management is repeatedly framed less as a settled practice than as a research frontier: the recurring call is to move away from passive, one-way ``unilateral'' subsurface drainage toward systems that give farmers active, location-specific control over the water table and over the coupled irrigation--drainage water balance **[CITATION CHECKED: Ayars2006b]**. Across arid, semiarid, humid, and irrigated command-area settings, authors converge on a small set of open problems: (i) developing design criteria, structures, and decision-support tools for \emph{active} rather than passive management \parencite{Ayars2006b,Youssef2023,Saadat2017}; (ii) automating and data-driving water-balance control through sensors and models \parencite{Youssef2023,Ikonen2023,Isomäki2024}; (iii) coordinating irrigation with drainage adjustments, including subirrigation embedded in regional water systems \parencite{Wahba2005,deWit2022,deWit2024}; (iv) sustaining drainage-water reuse and salinity control while protecting downstream water quality \parencite{WESTCOT1988,Sharma1998,Ayars2015}; (v) adapting design to changing crop water needs, climate extremes, and irrigation modernization \parencite{Rui2024,Ritzema2007,Ziaeifar2025}; and (vi) resolving the institutional, economic, and participatory barriers that condition adoption \parencite{Ritzema2011,Castellano2019,Qureshi2008}. A cross-cutting message is that many recommendations remain qualitative and site-specific, and that long-term, multi-scale evidence is still lacking. Kesicka \textcite{Kesicka2023b} frames replacing unilateral drainage with methods of controlling drainage outflows as a current global challenge, and continued research is broadly expected to keep refining drainage techniques to optimize agricultural water use.

section: Controlled Drainage and Irrigation Water Management
subsection: Design criteria for changing crops, climate, and irrigation modernization
claim_paragraph: Design intensity itself is an open research question. **[CITATION CHECKED: Dialameh2025]** note that where adjusting drain spacing is infeasible, other water-management practices may be needed to mitigate increased drought severity, and that future design decisions may need to account for management and economic factors beyond those modeled. \textcite{Singh2009} caution that reduced drain spacing would require increased capacity across the entire drainage network---a factor for future network design---and would heighten the emphasis on best management practices to reduce nutrient loss. \textcite{Castellano2019} advocate a systems approach integrating drainage, crop--soil processes, and nutrient-loss-reduction practices to design drained cropping systems that mitigate and adapt to climate change, and call for identifying long-term cost savings (e.g., greater fertilizer nitrogen-use efficiency) that could offset the higher installation costs of altered drain depth and spacing. \textcite{Strock2011} recommend detailed analysis with DRAINMOD or another drainage model to develop optimum drainage rates and drain spacing across U.S. locations and soils. Fundamental design questions persist about which soil parameters are most critical and what confidence intervals are required for each \parencite{Ayars2015}, and about proper design guidelines for specific geologic conditions such as the Mid-Atlantic states \parencite{SHIRMOHAMMADI1995}. The optimum design is repeatedly framed as a cost--benefit balance \parencite{HARDJOAMIDJOJO1982}, and irrigation is emphasized as necessary to reduce deficit soil-water conditions where drainage alone cannot raise yields \parencite{HARDJOAMIDJOJO1982}.

section: Controlled Drainage and Irrigation Water Management
subsection: Crop, soil, and agronomic research directions
claim_paragraph: Refining the biophysical targets of control is an active frontier. The required water-table depth must be refined by crop, soil type, and season, and it must be verified that shallow drains can control root-zone salinity over the long term before farmer implementation \parencite{Christen2001b}. Root-development responses to tile drainage---and consequent effects on plant water uptake during drought---need further study **[CITATION CHECKED: Nash2015b]**. Further work is needed on drainage and desalination in unsaturated soil and on the design/engineering of tile drainage under drip irrigation \parencite{Chen2021}. Winter crops that leave soils bare during hot summers warrant more investigation, and longer research is needed on CD in sugarcane \parencite{Akram2013}. On soils with high perched water tables, progress depends on understanding factors limiting crop growth and developing improved strategies, potentially including mole drainage or increasing drainable porosity by loosening soil above the drain \parencite{Muirhead1996}; strategies to reduce flow to shallow subsurface drains and more sustainable practices are also needed \parencite{Muirhead1996}. Soil-management options such as subsoiling, deep-rooted cropping, and drainage trenches are viable short-term solutions \parencite{Guedessou2021}. \textcite{Manik2019} outline a waterlogging-tolerance agenda: increasing soil-profile de-watering through soil-improvement and agronomic strategies, greater specificity of management--environment and management--management interactions, discovering new non-oxygen-associated QTLs, testing their effectiveness alone and combined under multiple constraints, evaluating agronomic/yield/quality effects, and developing management packages for varieties with diverse tolerance genes---plus cost/benefit comparison of different drainage strategies. Salt-tolerant germplasm, groundwater-abstraction regulation, and crop diversification (e.g., salt-tolerant medicinal and aromatic species) are recommended \parencite{Qureshi2008}, as are salt-tolerant crops such as eucalyptus or phreatophytes and drainage installation where leaching with poor-quality water is infeasible \parencite{Sarwar2001}. Supplementary measures---gypsum application, salt-resistant varieties, and irrigation-efficiency improvement---are needed to enhance subsurface-drainage benefits \parencite{Ritzema2008b}. Pressurized irrigation and reduced irrigation amounts are recommended to lessen waterlogging and drainage needs \parencite{Khorramian2022}, more research is needed on leaching requirements for modern irrigation in heavy clay soil \parencite{Mahmoud2021}, and alternatives such as surface irrigation and improved fertility management alongside proper drainage should be weighed for claypan soils \parencite{MOSTAGHIMI1989}.

section: Controlled Drainage and Irrigation Water Management
subsection: Modeling, monitoring, and long-term evaluation
claim_paragraph: Authors repeatedly call for stronger modeling, longer records, and better monitoring. Long-term studies are broadly needed to validate active-management approaches \parencite{Ayars2006b}, and the long-term effects of CD---especially in arid and semiarid regions---remain understudied \parencite{Wang2020c}. \textcite{Wang2020c} further urge defining soils by internationally accepted standards (or fuller descriptions), investigating CD from a climate standpoint, combining future designs with proposed underlying mechanisms for more reliable evaluation, and classifying situations to understand CD's contribution to total nitrogen in drainage water. Watershed-scale water-table-management research is needed to develop best management practices and select the best water-management scenario, and more flexible CD schemes may alter impacts on tile drainage, surface runoff, and shallow-water-table days \parencite{Golmohammadi2016}. \textcite{Kim2023} present the SWAT-tile model as opening opportunities for water-quality research and tile-depth installation, and as a viable strategy for managing flow and nitrate transport at field and watershed scales. Steady/transient simulations of steady recharge are framed as an initial step toward broader analyses that could propose conceptual modifications to traditional design for water-quality control \parencite{GRISMER1993}. Regional modeling calls include extending simulation periods to capture dynamic equilibrium and long-term sustainability, completing calibration of groundwater flow-and-transport models, and refining field data on irrigation efficiencies, canal seepage, drainage, and return flows \parencite{Triana2010}. Environmental monitoring and decision-support systems should be designed at project onset to work hand-in-hand with drainage operations, built bottom-up and documented progressively **[CITATION CHECKED: Quinn2009]**. Additional model-supported directions include using a different field-scale hydrologic model to evaluate CD's yield effect \parencite{BinShokrana2023} and exploring interactive tools such as DRAINFRAME \parencite{Gopalakrishnan2007}. Remote sensing to detect drainage and salinity needs---via drones and satellite imagery \parencite{Yannopoulos2020}, and refined, upscaled remote-sensing assessment of waterlogged/saline areas \parencite{Gopalakrishnan2007}---is another data frontier. Reviewing prior research and projects is urged to avoid trial-and-error and reduce failure risk in future rehabilitation/construction \parencite{Valipour2014}.

section: Controlled Drainage and Irrigation Water Management
subsection: Drainage-water reuse, salinity, and water-quality frontiers
claim_paragraph: Reuse-focused research spans agronomy, scheduling, and safety. \textcite{WESTCOT1988} list needs for site-specific load--flow relationships for trace elements, expanded knowledge of germination and early-seedling salinity tolerance, ratings of crops' use of saline groundwater, improved irrigation scheduling that lets farmers meet crop ET from a portion of the high water table while minimizing upward salt flow, wider commercial applicability of direct drainage-water reuse, better understanding of bioaccumulation and trace-element immobilization in evaporation basins, and caution in reusing salts until safety is better known. Field guidance likewise remains provisional: substituting drainage water up to 9~dS/m for wheat at post-germination stages where non-saline canal water is scarce, then reverting to non-saline canal water for one or two years after 6--7 years of drainage-water use, with careful case-by-case evaluation \parencite{Sharma1998}. Keeping drainage effluent as low as possible by improving irrigation efficiency and blending fresh and drainage water, plus disposal options such as farm ponds for storing and evaporating drainage water, are proposed \parencite{Datta2002}, as is minimizing effluent by improving irrigation efficiency and farm-level reuse while maintaining soil health \parencite{Qureshi2008}. Autumn or winter irrigation combined with subsurface pipe drainage is suggested for leaching excess soil salt \parencite{Dou2022}, seasonal groundwater undulation is deemed necessary to prevent salt accumulation \parencite{Mirlas2021}, and proper irrigation schemes---shifting from traditional to drip irrigation---are recommended to sustain growth while flushing salts \parencite{Mirlas2021}. Root-zone salinity and the water table should be kept low, at least in early growth stages \parencite{Singh2019}. Non-conventional treatment via engineered in-stream and off-stream wetlands is being explored at pilot scales \parencite{AbdelDayem2007}, and drainage water outflow is argued to require treatment before discharge to surface or groundwater \parencite{Filipovic2015}. Emerging soil-remediation directions include exploring acidic biochar in saline-alkaline soils and its synergy with subsurface drainage, plus plant-remediation desalination and other collaborative measures \parencite{Liu2025f}. Reclamation innovations include harvesting subsurface-drainage water in dryland/semiarid sites for livestock, windbreaks, gardens, or salt leaching, and establishing alfalfa in saline-seep areas fitted with engineered drainage wells \parencite{Steppuhn2017}. Progressive-flooding and progressive-leaching methodologies still require experimental validation and extension to finer-textured soils \parencite{Youngs2000}. Salinity control is argued to belong within a basin-wide salt-balance context **[CITATION CHECKED: Qureshi2008]**, and comprehensive assessment of waterlogging and salinity together (rather than separately) is recommended to yield more reliable findings \parencite{Valipour2014}.

section: Controlled Drainage and Irrigation Water Management
subsection: Economics, institutions, and adoption
claim_paragraph: Institutional and participatory needs are pervasive. Recommendations include shifting from standardized to flexible, location-specific solutions reflecting stakeholder preferences \parencite{Ritzema2011,Ritzema2016,Ritzema2023}; balancing top-down against bottom-up through participatory management across planning, design, installation, operation, and maintenance \parencite{Ritzema2016}; improving farmer participation throughout the drainage-infrastructure lifecycle \parencite{Ritzema2023}; and better identifying stakeholders' needs, preferences, and willingness to contribute while linking their tacit knowledge with researchers' explicit knowledge \parencite{Ritzema2011}. Capacity development---integrating research, education, and advisory services---is emphasized \parencite{Ritzema2016}, along with the substantial education and policy change needed to lower adoption barriers \parencite{Castellano2019}, public/institutional education programs on drainage and water-table management \parencite{SHIRMOHAMMADI1995}, and addressing negative perceptions that conflate agricultural drainage with wetland drainage before the application base can expand \parencite{THOMAS1995}. Scientists and policy institutions should help farmers adopt innovations through financial support and knowledge exchange \parencite{Kesicka2023b}. Governance recommendations include developing procedural/organizational frameworks and national or regional support groups, working groups for diverse agro-hydro-climatic regions, and multi-departmental coordination committees in command areas \parencite{Singh2019c}; enhanced inter-agency coordination for water allocation \parencite{Qureshi2008}; a dedicated state-level Drainage Division and national drainage institution, standardization of components, and promotion of private-sector reclamation and local SSD installation \parencite{Gopalakrishnan2007}; drainage policy papers with time-bound reclamation action plans \parencite{Ritzema2008b,Valipour2014}; and appropriate institutional arrangements for farmers' participation \parencite{Ritzema2008b}. Adaptive regulatory frameworks that promote local irrigation/drainage flexibility and grower innovation, communicate successes, recognize failures early, and disseminate information are recommended \parencite{Quinn2009}. Programs to create awareness and promote subsidies and micro-finance **[CITATION CHECKED: Satyanarayana2007]**, to convince farmers to clear drainage blockages and maintain systems \parencite{Manjunatha2004}, and to ensure participatory operation and maintenance for sustainability \parencite{Gopalakrishnan2007} round out the adoption agenda. Continued technical and financial support is deemed essential to sustain irrigated agriculture \parencite{Qureshi2008}, research in irrigated agriculture is ``not yet over'' \parencite{Ritzema2007}, and a participatory approach is demanded by changing socio-economic conditions \parencite{Ritzema2007}. Practical framing choices---outsourcing/privatizing drainage activities \parencite{AbdelDayem2007}, budgeting for certified local consultants to support decentralized design \parencite{Ritzema2023}, and switching from gravity to pumped drainage to enable reuse and shrink open-drain dimensions \parencite{Ritzema2023}---are also proposed. Large-scale drainage investment tied to adjusted irrigation planning is viewed as unavoidable in the long run \parencite{Sarwar2001}, and accumulated reclamation experience is expected to inform future developments worldwide \parencite{TeKrony2004}.

section: Tile Drainage Research Gaps and Modeling Needs
subsection: Model Structure, Routines, and Parameterisation
claim_paragraph: Some gaps concern the underlying physics of flow and solute movement. \textcite{Qi2018} suggest that the method of simulating subsurface water flow in the soil matrix should be revisited or replaced by a soil-matrix-potential-based Richards equation, and that the algorithm for particulate-phosphorus loss to tile drainage should be revisited. \textcite{Mohanty1998} argue that tile flow and conservative solute transport would perhaps be better interpreted and modelled with a three-dimensional model considering regional water and chemical management, and that more detailed consideration of regional hydrology and adjacent-bench irrigation/fertiliser scheduling is needed to improve prediction. \textcite{DeSchepper2015} report developing a larger-scale model to simulate seasonal variation in tile-drainage outflow with heterogeneities of clayey tills represented in greater detail, and argue that more realistic simulated water-flow patterns in heterogeneous drained fields are a cornerstone of future nutrient-transport modelling; they anticipate future work focusing on nutrient-transport modelling. **[CITATION CHECKED: Garrison1999]** propose that integrating spatial images of surface wetness (before emergence) and within-season vegetative index, coupled with final yield, will refine tile-model parameters, and that their tile-water and nitrogen-flow methods may found improved spatial representation of soil-water and nitrogen dynamics.

section: Tile Drainage Research Gaps and Modeling Needs
subsection: Overview
claim_paragraph: Despite decades of field and modelling work, the literature synthesised here converges on a shared diagnosis: our capacity to predict how subsurface (tile) drainage alters water, sediment, and nutrient export remains limited by sparse field verification, incomplete knowledge of where and how drains are installed, and process representations that are too coarse for the scales at which decisions are made. The recurring research frontier therefore spans four interlocking gaps. First, watershed-scale hydrologic effects of tiling must be assessed with both models and field observations, across events of all sizes and multiple landscapes, rather than inferred from single sites \parencite{Schilling2008,Sloan2017,Sloan2016}. Second, the spatial location, extent, and specifications of drainage networks are largely unknown, motivating calls for mapping, databases, and validated prediction of tile lines \parencite{Naz2009,Zhou2025,Valayamkunnath2020}. Third, existing agricultural models (APEX, DRAINMOD, SWAT, MIKE~SHE, and others) require improved tile, water-table, macropore, and phosphorus routines, together with careful treatment of parameter uncertainty when drainage specifications are unknown at calibration **[CITATION CHECKED: Nelson2018]**. Fourth, key transport processes---preferential and macropore flow, phosphorus source partitioning, sediment storage and exhaustion, and cold-season dynamics---remain underquantified and must be constrained with longer-term, higher-resolution monitoring \parencite{King2015,Grangeon2021,Trentman2020}. The subsections below organise the identified gaps, hypotheses, and methodological needs around these themes.

section: Watershed Modeling for Drainage Management
subsection: Integrated, adaptive, and stakeholder-connected modeling frameworks
claim_paragraph: A final cross-cutting frontier is methodological integration. \textcite{Dollinger2015} articulate perhaps the most explicit long-range vision: developing numerically explicit modeling approaches at the landscape scale that integrate and couple the major processes governing the provision of landscape services by ditches, optimizing the spatial arrangement of management practices according to catchment heterogeneity and ditch connectivity, and defining efficient multi-service maximization strategies informed by an a priori, stakeholder-valued ranking of services---while acquiring new knowledge on feedbacks between processes that have most often been studied in isolation. Better mapping of key ditch characteristics (hydraulic, vegetation, and sorption properties) and study of poorly understood processes such as pollutant sorption and degradation are prerequisites **[CITATION CHECKED: Herzon2008]**. Landscape-scale, integrated approaches tailored to local conditions---combining on-farm changes with off-site wetland and riparian restoration and attentive site- and landscape-level design and monitoring---are broadly endorsed \parencite{Blann2009}. Managing catchment nitrogen export is argued to require acknowledging groundwater as well as farm-scale losses and intercepting edge-of-field pathways such as tile and open drains, using stream-rehabilitation and drainage water management tools especially during wet periods \parencite{Goeller2019}. Truly integrated watershed management is said to require better information on the controlling processes---such as spatial groundwater-head distribution---that link topography--geology interactions to the drain fraction \parencite{Mahmood2023}. Coupled field--watershed models enable scenario analyses of water-table management not possible when component models are used separately, and, once tested, can evaluate environmentally sound management in cold regions \parencite{Dayyani2010}. Modeling frameworks should remain extensible---for example, modifying loading-estimation approaches to incorporate additional processes and pathways and the distribution of planting dates across a watershed \parencite{Basu2010}, and refining and dynamically estimating proposed indices through field calibration \parencite{Tao2025}. Detailed, site-specific nutrient-management planning is recommended to handle the interactions between site hydrology and management practices \parencite{Kurz2005}. More catchment-scale research on water quality, wetland carbon sequestration, habitat quality, and cultural and educational services---and on the effects of upgrading existing drainage infrastructure rather than only new installations---is needed to fully populate these integrated frameworks \parencite{Mitchell2022}. Ultimately, tighter interaction among stakeholders, experimentalists, and modelers is identified as essential to make watershed modeling a credible basis for prioritizing drainage water management \parencite{Wang2020b,Kröger2013}.

section: Watershed Modeling for Drainage Management
subsection: Practice-scale modeling frontiers: wetlands, controlled drainage, and drainage water recycling
claim_paragraph: For controlled and managed drainage, future research should track complete water and nutrient budgets within and across field boundaries \parencite{Shedekar2021} and investigate effects on water and nutrients lost by other pathways---surface runoff, preferential flow, groundwater recharge, and biological uptake \parencite{Ross2016}. Additional research on drainage water management should span a range of soil textures, cropping systems, and climates and evaluate effects on surface and subsurface phosphorus dynamics \parencite{King2022}, with greater attention to phosphorus given the paucity of research and to combinations with practices such as sub-irrigation \parencite{Ross2016}. Whether drainage water management within channelized streams can restore more natural hydrology---and how such hydrologic change affects headwater biogeochemistry---requires comprehensive, integrated hydrology--water-quality--ecology assessment \parencite{King2009}. The potential of controlled tile drainage to reduce downstream flood risk by significantly reducing watershed-scale stream discharge is highlighted for further development \parencite{Sunohara2015}, and control structures on subsurface tile drainage, together with wetland restoration, are noted as promising means of storing more water on the landscape in spring \parencite{Dalzell2018}. Long-term monitoring with moisture sensors and automated systems is sought to improve drainage water recycling efficiency in tile-drained landscapes \parencite{Kaur2021}, and models such as DRAINMOD-DWR are needed to aid the design and management of recycling systems, supported by longer-term performance monitoring across weather, soil, and design conditions and by economic optimization of implementation and management costs \parencite{Moursi2024}. Full-scale field studies of drainage water recycling and saturated buffers under varied conditions, and study of emerging water-quality-wetland types such as reconstructed oxbows, round out the practice-scale agenda **[CITATION CHECKED: Mitchell2023]**. Restoration of multipurpose oxbows should continue with careful monitoring to determine whether observed relationships with tiles are representative, including further study of temperature differences among oxbow types \parencite{Leberg2024}, and installed weirs and additional floodplain work are being used to resolve surface- and groundwater-flow directions at restored oxbow sites \parencite{Schilling2017}. Edge-of-field filters and phosphorus-sorbing materials warrant testing at higher runoff loadings and in both surface and subsurface pathways \parencite{Plach2023}, filter and grass strips need evaluation of dormant-season loading and vegetation harvest \parencite{Holly2016,Vallée2015}, and the long-term effectiveness and wider deployment of small constructed wetlands and grass strips deserve continued evaluation \parencite{Vallée2015}.

section: Watershed Modeling for Drainage Management
subsection: Data, monitoring, and long-term records to constrain models
claim_paragraph: Nearly every modeling ambition is bottlenecked by data. \textcite{Christianson2015} call for more intensive year-round monitoring in some locations, improved monitoring of newly drained areas, ditch-drained areas, and surface intakes, more long-term studies with coordinated controls across multiple sites and years, and continued construction of region-specific drainage water-quality data for underrepresented regions---adding that understanding drainage-design impacts grows more important as aging infrastructure is replaced and upgraded. Long-term records are singled out as necessary to disentangle the possibly counteracting effects of land management and climate change on biogeochemical and hydrological processes, with the corollary that evaluating policy measures will demand patience \parencite{Bauwe2020}. Long-term, catchment-scale study is deemed essential to understand management and climate-change impacts \parencite{Kelley2017}, and the establishment and use of long-term studies tracking the effects of management changes on runoff phosphorus losses is a standing recommendation \parencite{Gillingham2000}. Follow-up investigations of implemented strategies are described as critical for adaptive management **[CITATION CHECKED: Schilling2012b]**, and long-term watershed data are advocated as the foundation for models that target high-pollution-potential areas and project watershed responses to BMP implementation \parencite{Lemke2011}.

section: Soil Macroporosity and Drainage-Induced Structure
subsection: Overview
claim_paragraph: Subsurface (tile) drainage is not a hydraulically passive intervention: by lowering and stabilising the water table it reorganises the soil pore system, its aeration status, and the pathways along which water and solutes move to the drain. The evidence assembled here establishes several well-supported propositions. First, rapid delivery of water and surface-applied solutes to tile drains is governed by a small volume of continuous macropores---principally earthworm burrows, shrinkage cracks, root channels, and old installation scars---rather than by uniform matrix flow \parencite{Shipitalo2004,Stamm2002,Villholth1998,Zehe2001,Nielsen2015,Petersen2012}. Second, these flow-active pathways and the broader pore network vary systematically both with depth and, more weakly, with lateral position relative to the drain line, so that the bulk soil directly above a drain is often more conductive and more biologically active than the inter-drain zone \parencite{Shipitalo2004,Alakukku2010,Nielsen2015,Petersen2012,Montagne2009}. Third, sustained drainage measurably alters static structural properties---reducing bulk density, increasing air-filled porosity and gas diffusivity, and improving saturated hydraulic conductivity---although the magnitude of these changes is modest and frequently smaller than that of tillage or of the passage of time since installation **[CITATION CHECKED: Frankl2023]**. Fourth, mechanical structural interventions coupled to drainage---mole drainage and subsoiling---create large, effective, but time-limited pore networks that dominate flow in heavy clays \parencite{MULLER1988,HARRIS1993,PLAMENAC1988,JHA1995,Castanheira2010}. Finally, over decades drainage accelerates pedogenic processes---eluviation, clay translocation, and iron/manganese redistribution---leaving a spatially heterogeneous, partly irreversible imprint on soil morphology \parencite{Montagne2008,Montagne2010,Montagne2013,Mercier2000,YliHalla2009}. The lines of evidence range from field tracer and dye/smoke experiments through soil physical sampling and micromorphology to numerical dual-domain modelling, and they converge on a consistent mechanistic picture in which a structured, connectivity-limited macropore system is the central control on drained-soil behaviour.

section: Nitrate and Nutrient Loss via Drainage
subsection: Overview
claim_paragraph: The evidence also converges on a suite of mitigation strategies with quantified, mechanistically coherent effects. Drainage water management (controlled drainage, subirrigation, and drainage water recycling) reliably reduces drainage volume and nitrate load, typically in proportion to the flow reduction, while often maintaining or increasing yield \parencite{Skaggs2010,Youssef2018,Wu2025,Madramootoo2024}. Edge-of-field and beyond-the-field practices, constructed wetlands, denitrification bioreactors and walls, saturated buffers, two-stage ditches, ditch weirs, riparian zones, and filter strips, remove nitrate mainly by denitrification and reduce phosphorus and sediment with more variable efficiency **[CITATION CHECKED: Hodaj2017]**. In-field practices, principally cover crops and nutrient management, cut tile nitrate loss substantially at the tile scale but show attenuated, scale-dependent signals at the watershed outlet \parencite{Hanrahan2018,Speir2022,Gentry2014}. This section synthesizes these consolidated findings, organized around the magnitude and pathways of loss, the hydrologic and land-management controls that drive them, and the drainage-management, edge-of-field, and watershed-scale strategies shown to abate them, together with the salinity, trace-element, and pesticide dimensions of drainage water quality.

section: Nitrate and Nutrient Loss via Drainage
subsection: Salinity, Trace Elements, Pesticides, and Contaminant Dynamics
claim_paragraph: Drainage of acid sulphate soils is a distinct hazard: subsurface drainage was a major cause of stream pH declines to near or below $4.0$ (and $3.0$ in ditches), elevating Al and other metals, with controlled pipe drainage recommended over in-stream liming \parencite{Osterholm2005,Åström2005}. Pesticides appear in drainage within a month of application as a general rule, with losses tied to application quantity and compound properties; highest concentrations occur at plot scale and dilute downstream \parencite{Tournebize2012}. Constructed wetlands and small grass-strip wetlands remove pesticides with efficiency governed by sorption ($K_{oc}$), degradation ($DT_{50}$), and residence time, sometimes with negative efficiencies \parencite{Tournebize2017,Vallée2015}. Persistent degradates such as metolachlor ESA remained in groundwater up to $18$~years but did not migrate far, and no detections exceeded MCLs \parencite{Puckett2005}; drainage increased nitrate but decreased atrazine relative to runoff-only conditions \parencite{SPALING1995}. Isotopic and geochemical tracers resolve sources and pathways: combined stable isotopes and fecal markers showed nitrate sources vary with hydrological stage and that soils play a determinant role in nitrate formation and transfer \parencite{Briand2017}, and multi-tracer analysis distinguished shallow chloride- and nitrate-rich groundwater from regional carbonate-aquifer water in the Wabash headwaters \parencite{Frisbee2022}. Direct effluent bypass through mole-pipe drains contributed disproportionately to pollutant loads (\emph{c.} $81\%$ of \emph{E. coli}, $72\%$ of ammonium-N, $55\%$ of P) despite averaging only $\sim0.7\%$ of applied effluent, motivating storage and slower application **[CITATION CHECKED: Monaghan2004]**.

section: Nitrate and Nutrient Loss via Drainage
subsection: Drainage Water Management: Controlled Drainage and Subirrigation
claim_paragraph: The timing of control governs efficacy: DRAINMOD analysis identified $1$--$15$~March as the most effective window, when CD could reduce subsurface outflow and nitrate-N losses by up to $100\%$ and retain up to $22$~kg~NO$_3$-N~ha$^{-1}$, whereas April starts resembled free drainage \parencite{Kesicka2023c}. Lithuanian CD reduced monthly outflow $55$--$80\%$, inorganic-N load $42$--$77\%$, and TP load $34$--$72\%$ **[CITATION CHECKED: Povilaitis2018]**. Modelled shallow drainage outperformed CD for nitrogen (reducing N loss $40\%$ vs. $26\%$ long-term) with minimal yield penalty \parencite{Craft2018}. Trade-offs are recognized: CD can increase surface DRP and TP losses that partly offset subsurface benefits \parencite{King2022,Wu2025}, and controlled drainage--subirrigation was predicted to raise runoff N ($+340\%$) and sediment N ($+118\%$) even while cutting leaching $35\%$, for a net $17.8\%$ reduction in combined non-point N \parencite{SHIRMOHAMMADI1995}. Greenhouse-gas responses are mixed but generally not adverse: N$_2$O fluxes under CD were $49\%$ higher than free drainage in three years and up to $43\%$ lower in three others \parencite{Madramootoo2024}. Drainage-management alone often fails to lower concentrations even when it lowers loads via volume reduction \parencite{Grenon2023,Wesström2014}. Automatic CD/subirrigation outperformed traditional CD, reducing N losses up to $27\%$, increasing plant uptake, and saving $28$--$77\%$ of subirrigation water \parencite{Abdelbaki2025}. Subirrigation lysimeters in Iran cut drainage nitrate concentrations by $74$--$84\%$ and improved yield and water-use efficiency \parencite{Noory2009}, and Swedish controlled drainage/subirrigation reduced NO$_3$-N, TN, PO$_4$-P, and TP losses to about $40\%$ of conventional while raising yield and N uptake \parencite{Wesström2014}.

section: Nitrate and Nutrient Loss via Drainage
subsection: Edge-of-Field and Beyond-the-Field Practices
claim_paragraph: Constructed wetlands treating drainage are extensively documented as effective nitrate sinks, with denitrification the dominant mechanism. Across drained French watersheds, nitrate removal averaged $\sim42\%$ (up to $40$--$90\%$), dominated by denitrification ($93\%$) over plant uptake ($7\%$), and devoting $\sim1\%$ of contributing area to a wetland can realistically achieve $50\%$ removal, with hydraulic residence time the priority control \parencite{Tournebize2017}. Iowa wetlands reduced incoming nitrate concentrations $49\%$ and loads $\sim61$~kg~day$^{-1}$, with performance varying by hydrology ($23$--$65\%$) \parencite{Drake2018}; a Minnesota wetland removed $67\%$ of tile nitrate over four years, mostly via infiltration to shallow groundwater \parencite{Gordon2021}; and another removed $68\%$ of nitrate and $\sim76\%$ of phosphorus, with plant harvest the primary P-removal route \parencite{Lenhart2016}. Illinois wetlands retained $36$--$37\%$ of nitrate and total N and over half of P fractions, and $\sim450$~ha of wetland were estimated necessary to cut watershed N loading $46\%$ \parencite{Kovacic2006}. New Zealand wetlands occupying $1$--$2\%$ of catchment area removed $16$--$63\%$ of nitrate-N loads but performed poorly for P, sometimes exporting more TP than received **[CITATION CHECKED: Tanner2005b]**. Wetland performance is strongly a function of hydraulic loading rate, residence time, temperature, and inlet concentration: a first-order areal model with median $k_{20}=25$~m~yr$^{-1}$ and temperature coefficient $1.106$ best represents whole-system behaviour, and no single-number design is adequate \parencite{Kadlec2012,Kalcic2018}. A German wetland retained only $2.9\%$ of TN over four years, but retention reached $\sim80\%$ when loads were low and residence time exceeded $20$~days at temperatures above $8\,^{\circ}$C \parencite{Steidl2019}. Meta-analysis reported mean cropland-drainage removals of $23.7\%$ TN and $30.3\%$ nitrate-N but negative mean removals for ammonium and TP, underscoring variable P and ammonium behaviour \parencite{Messer2021}.

section: Nitrate and Nutrient Loss via Drainage
subsection: Watershed-Scale Assessment, Modelling, and Reduction Strategies
claim_paragraph: Watershed-planning studies show that meeting large reduction goals requires combining in-field and edge-of-field practices. In the Mississippi basin, nitrogen-management practices alone were insufficient (improved fertilizer management and cover crops together cut delivered loads $30.2\%$), but a full suite of N-management plus N-removal practices reached the $45\%$ target while converting under $6\%$, and as little as $2.5\%$, of cropland when practices were combined and targeted \parencite{McLellan2015}. High-resolution LiDAR-based planning identified scenarios achieving $34$--$39\%$ nitrate reduction while removing $<5\%$ of cropland, with cover crops and nutrient-removal wetlands common to the best scenarios **[CITATION CHECKED: Tomer2015]**. Long-term simulation suggested DWM could plausibly help meet Iowa's $41\%$ reduction goal \parencite{Craft2018}, and a Czech pilot designed measures reducing drainage nitrate load $24\%$ across $38\%$ of the drained area \parencite{Kvítek2023}. Yet watershed-scale evidence also cautions that traditional surface-water BMPs may be inadequate over tile drainage: seven years of increased strip-till, grassed waterways, and stream buffers produced no measurable change in nitrate, phosphorus, sediment, or hydrology, because they did not intercept subsurface flow, which must be a design priority \parencite{Lemke2011}. Ecosystem-service framing shows drainage modernization can sharply reduce migratory-bird habitat (up to $87\%$ for dabbling ducks) while paired water-quality wetlands substantially reduce nitrate export and partially offset habitat loss, benefiting diving ducks most \parencite{Mitchell2022,Mitchell2025}. Managed and semi-natural ditch networks themselves provide biodiversity, water-purification, and nutrient-retention functions that depend on vegetation, morphology, and maintenance, with no single maintenance regime optimizing all services \parencite{Dollinger2015,Herzon2008}. Field observations that subsurface drainage installation did not measurably alter soil-health metrics or soil organic carbon over two years, against strong seasonal and interannual variation, further temper expectations of rapid in-soil change \parencite{Sherbine2023,Huang2023}.

section: Tile Drain Nitrate Loss Model Calibration
subsection: The DRAINMOD family of drainage and nitrogen models
claim_paragraph: Nitrate simulation with the DRAINMOD suite is generally satisfactory at annual and cumulative scales but weaker at monthly and daily resolution. In Minnesota, annual nitrate loss was reproduced with a mean deviation of 2.16\,kg\,ha$^{-1}$ and $R^2 = 0.98$, while corn yield was captured less precisely ($R^2 = 0.69$) \parencite{Zhao2000}. In North Carolina, monthly nitrate-N loss was poorly matched (EF of 0.48 for the calibration plot and near zero or negative for others), but annual losses were well predicted for most plots (yearly EF up to 0.92) and cumulative six-year losses were predicted very accurately, with errors of only $-1.3$ to $4.0\%$ \parencite{Youssef2006}. Indian applications gave nitrogen-load NSE of 0.82--0.84 with cumulative predicted losses of 32.15 and 28.77\,kg\,ha$^{-1}$ against observed 33.07 and 26.88\,kg\,ha$^{-1}$ \parencite{Dar2022}, and daily nitrate-N loads with NSE and $R^2$ of 0.66--0.70 (calibration) and 0.88 (validation), with mean daily concentrations of 13.64 versus 12.9 and 11.09 versus 11.19\,mg\,L$^{-1}$ \parencite{Dar2025}. DRAINMOD-N reproduced nitrate-N losses in surface runoff with high accuracy but was less accurate for drain-outflow losses, tending to overestimate them during colder months and freeze--thaw periods; it nonetheless gave reasonable predictions across tillage and intercropping treatments not explicitly represented as inputs \parencite{Yang2007}. Two-year total nitrate-N loss errors of 1.32--1.40\,kg\,ha$^{-1}$ (calibration) and $-1.64$ to 0.97\,kg\,ha$^{-1}$ (validation) were reported for DRAINMOD 5.1 in Canada \parencite{Wang2006c}, and monthly nitrate-N losses were matched with $R^2 = 0.90$--$0.94$ under free drainage and sub-irrigation \parencite{Dayyani2010b}. Simulated annual nitrogen process rates (mineralisation, nitrification, denitrification, volatilisation, deposition) fell within reported literature ranges \parencite{Salazar2009}, and studies in Minnesota consistently indicated a nitrogen budget surplus, implying scope to reduce fertiliser rates and thereby drainage nitrate losses **[CITATION CHECKED: Ale2013]**.

section: Tile Drain Nitrate Loss Model Calibration
subsection: Recurring performance patterns across models
claim_paragraph: Calibration studies repeatedly identify soil-hydraulic and water-flow parameters as controlling tile-drain and nitrate predictions. Measured soil hydraulic properties substantially outperformed default texture-class values \parencite{Ma2007c,Ahuja2007}, with lateral saturated conductivity in and just above the tile layer the most sensitive parameter \parencite{Ma2007c} and Brooks--Corey parameters, saturated conductivity, and drainable porosity most sensitive for tile flow \parencite{Ahmed2007}. Soil field capacity was the single most sensitive parameter for nitrate loss and flow-weighted concentration in HERMES and RZWQM, through its control on denitrification and mineralisation **[CITATION CHECKED: Gillette2018]**. Precipitation was the most sensitive driver of nitrogen loading, while slope governed sediment and particulate-N loss and fertiliser rate governed nitrate leaching \parencite{Deng2011}; moisture and decay-rate limiters strongly affected nitrate loads in FLUSH \parencite{Salo2015}; and drain-depth and drain-spacing parameters (DDRAIN, SDRAIN) were moderately sensitive for streamflow in SWAT \parencite{Moriasi2012}. Constraining models with soft data and multiple objectives lowered nominal efficiencies but produced more realistic water budgets and yields \parencite{Nelson2018}, and companion soil-moisture calibration was shown to be essential for accurate yield simulation \parencite{Wang2016}. Auxiliary tools such as the modified Checkbook water-balance model further improved in-field soil-moisture-deficit estimates under shallow water tables by adding upward flux and subsurface drainage \parencite{Kolars2019}.

section: Tile Drain Nitrate Loss Model Calibration
subsection: Overview
claim_paragraph: Simulation models are the principal tools for quantifying subsurface (tile) drainage flow and nitrate-N loss and for extrapolating short field experiments across weather, soils, cropping systems, and management. The body of calibration and validation studies synthesised here spans several model families: the process-based DRAINMOD suite (DRAINMOD, DRAINMOD-N, DRAINMOD-N\,II, DRAINMOD 5.1/6.1, and the coupled DRAINMOD-DSSAT); the Root Zone Water Quality Model and its variants (RZWQM, RZWQM2, RZWQM2-P, the RZWQM--DSSAT hybrid, and RZ-SHAW); the watershed-scale Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT) with successive tile-drainage and nitrogen routines, together with the related APEX model; cropping-system and biogeochemical models (APSIM, DNDC, \textit{ecosys}, HERMES, WHCNS, HYDRUS, FLUSH, CERES-Maize, and PNM); field-scale nutrient models such as ADAPT; and a growing set of statistical, regression, and machine-learning surrogates **[CITATION CHECKED: Luo2010]**.

section: Tile Drain Nitrate Loss Model Calibration
subsection: Management insights from calibrated models
claim_paragraph: Calibrated models consistently show that shallower drains and wider spacing reduce tile flow and nitrate loss, generally at modest yield cost. Reducing drain depth from 1.5 to 0.9\,m lowered simulated tile flow from 207 to 191\,mm and nitrate loss from 34.0 to 29.4\,kg\,ha$^{-1}$, and widening spacing from 27 to 60\,m reduced flow from 205 to 182\,mm and nitrate loss from 33.8 to 28.4\,kg\,ha$^{-1}$ \parencite{Moriasi2013}. Widening spacing from 27 to 40\,m cut nitrate loss from about 45 to 22\,kg\,ha$^{-1}$ with only a 7\% yield reduction \parencite{Nangia2010c}, and shallower depths reduced nitrate loss more than wider spacing for fine-textured soils \parencite{Davis2000}. Field and simulation studies in Illinois confirmed that plots with 18.3 and 24.4\,m spacing had lower drain flow and better nitrate retention than 12.2\,m spacing while maintaining or increasing yield \parencite{Hwang2024}. Scenario analyses further indicate optimal designs balancing yield and losses---for example, 1.3\,m depth with 42\,m spacing in India \parencite{Dar2025}, 28\,m spacing for a Minnesota clay loam **[CITATION CHECKED: Zhao2000]**, 1.2\,m depth with 24\,m spacing for the northern Corn Belt \parencite{Luo2010}, and wider spacing being environmentally preferable for nitrate under warming \parencite{Ziaeifar2025}. Increasing tile depth raised tile flow and, under physically consistent routines, tile nitrate load, whereas an inconsistent routine failed to reproduce this relationship \parencite{Kim2023,Bauwe2016}.

section: Phosphorus Loss Pathways and Soil Controls
subsection: Dissolved and Particulate Phosphorus Fractions and Bioavailability
claim_paragraph: A central state-of-knowledge finding is that PP is frequently the dominant P form in tile drainage, contrary to the earlier presumption that filtration by the soil profile leaves subsurface water dissolved-dominated. In Finnish clay soils, PP was the grand-mean 92\% of TP in both surface runoff and drainage, and most PP (93\%) was nondesorbable \parencite{Uusitalo2001}; across sites, PP comprised 73--94\% of runoff P \parencite{Uusitalo2003}. At Rothamsted's Broadbalk drains, PP averaged 54\% of TP (vs.\ 36\% for molybdate-reactive P) and reached 81.1\% on individual plots, with PP strongly linearly related to particulate matter (PM), which reached $\sim$0.6~g~L$^{-1}$ \parencite{Lu2003,Lu2004}. PP dominated TP export in both tile drainage and surface runoff in Ontario (though DRP:TP was higher in surface runoff) \parencite{VanEsbroeck2016}, made up most of drainage TP in Massachusetts \parencite{Millar2025}, and dominated Danish catchment losses (55--71\% of TP at three of four catchments) **[CITATION CHECKED: Grant1996]**. Catchment monitoring likewise showed drainage TP dominated by PP (only 39.8\% as DRP) with PP losses exceeding dissolved losses \parencite{Brendel2019}, and level Dutch grassland lost nutrients dominated by particulate forms via trenches and pipe drains \parencite{vanderSalm2012}. Over 80\% of predicted surface and subsurface P losses were particulate in an Ohio simulation \parencite{Askar2021b}, and pasture P export in New Zealand was $\sim$80\% particulate-associated \parencite{Gillingham2000}. Even where TP was small, PP dominated: a Finnish controlled-drainage peat field lost only 0.30~kg~P~ha$^{-1}$~yr$^{-1}$ of TP but 71\% as PP \parencite{Pham2023}.

section: Phosphorus Loss Pathways and Soil Controls
subsection:
Partitioning of Phosphorus Losses Between Surface Runoff and
Subsurface Drainage
claim_paragraph: The dominance of tiles is not universal, and the counter-examples define the conditions under which surface runoff prevails. In snowmelt-affected clay (vertisolic) landscapes of the northern Great Plains, overland flow contributed 72--89\% of runoff and $>95\%$ of annual SRP and TP losses, because tiles were decoupled from the surface by frozen ground and carried water only in wetter periods; SRP and TP were 600\% and 500\% greater in overland flow than tile flow \parencite{Kokulan2019b,Kokulan2021}. Surface runoff was also the major pathway for sediment, TP, and soluble P (though not nitrate) under Minnesota tillage systems \parencite{Zhao2001}, was the dominant P pathway from perennial pastures in Victoria when runoff occurred **[CITATION CHECKED: Melland2008]**, and modelling of an Ohio field attributed 78\% of predicted TP to surface runoff \parencite{Askar2021b}. In flooded paddy systems, surface runoff exceeded subsurface pathways for P during rice growth, and shallow subsurface drainage lowered TP loss mainly by reducing flooding \parencite{DarziNaftchali2016}. Thus pathway partitioning is strongly modulated by climate (snowmelt vs.\ rain-driven), soil texture, and drainage design rather than being a fixed property.

section: Phosphorus Loss Pathways and Soil Controls
subsection: Edge-of-Field Retention and Mitigation
claim_paragraph: The soil and pathway controls above define where mitigation must act, and a consolidated body of evidence quantifies edge-of-field practices---while emphasising trade-offs and site specificity. Drainage water (controlled) management can reduce loss by curtailing discharge: it cut dissolved P by 63\% and TP by 50\% in Minnesota \parencite{Kröger2013}, and managed drainage reduced tile ortho-P loss by 80\%, with more than half the reduction occurring in spring at similar drainage, suggesting enhanced crop P uptake \parencite{Nash2015c}. Controlled drainage with subirrigation reduced DRP, PP, and TP for low-P treatments but not for swine-manure compost \parencite{Zhang2015}, and reviews report TP reductions of 57\% and soluble-P reductions of 57--80\% \parencite{Elsayed2023}; however, controlled drainage can also raise DRP/TP or shift loss to surface runoff, and organic-soil concentrations may stay above limits even as loads fall \parencite{Grewal2025,Sadhukhan2019b,Grenon2021}. Blind inlets replacing tile risers reduced TP by up to 78\% and soluble P by up to 72\% \parencite{Kröger2013}, with 50--78\% TP and 65--72\% DRP reductions reported elsewhere \parencite{Singh2020c}. Subsurface placement and 4R management are highlighted as promising, with deep placement cutting DRP by 69--72\% \parencite{Wilson2019,Sharpley2019,Singh2020c}. Denitrifying bioreactors gave modest, variable DRP removal (median 12\% efficiency; outflow DRP less than half inflow) and occasionally acted as DRP sources under low summer flow \parencite{Bailon2025}. Filter media (Fe- and Al-based superior to Ca/Mg) and passive Fe-oxide resins target dissolved P, and P-sorbents can extend system lifetime under oxidising conditions **[CITATION CHECKED: Mendes2020]**. Constructed and vegetated systems retain P chiefly by particulate sedimentation, with retention of 27--100\% but strong dependence on hydraulic residence time, sorbent availability, and loading---systems can flip from sink to source during events \parencite{Mendes2020,Kröger2013,Singh2020c}. Vegetated ditches retained $\sim$44\% of inorganic P annually \parencite{Kröger2013}, drainage sediments and ditch beds shifted seasonally between P sink, source, and equilibrium \parencite{Ahiablame2010,Nguyen2002}, and routing $\sim$25\% of tile flow through a riparian buffer achieved near-complete removal of dissolved nutrients and sediment \parencite{Jacquemin2020}. Because buffers can bypass the root zone via tile loads and may saturate over time, modified, bypass-preventing designs and trap-and-treat ditches are emphasised \parencite{Mendes2020,Millar2025,Baulch2019}. Finally, tile drainage does not inevitably raise P export: under some conditions installing tiles reduced surface runoff and SRP losses without increasing TP export \parencite{Klaiber2020}, and in frozen vertisolic landscapes tile expansion may not exacerbate P (though it can raise N) \parencite{Kokulan2021}. Overall, effective P control depends on matching the right practice to site hydrology, connectivity, weather, and legacy P, and on recognising N--P trade-offs among conservation practices \parencite{King2015,Sharpley2019,Ni2020,Baulch2019,Wilson2019}.

section: Phosphorus Loss Pathways and Soil Controls
subsection: Management and Fertilisation History Controls
claim_paragraph: Tillage and residue management involve trade-offs between particulate and dissolved P. Conservation tillage, no-till, and cover crops were associated with higher subsurface DRP losses, while tillage increased PP and TSS **[CITATION CHECKED: Ni2020]**. No-till DRP losses were consistently greater and $\sim$60\% incidental, and lower PP at the no-till cover-crop site only partly offset higher DRP so that TP was only slightly lower there \parencite{Macrae2023}. Reduced tillage cut erosion but markedly increased DRP, so it should be paired with efficient subsurface drainage to minimise runoff \parencite{Koskiaho2002}; no-tillage had significantly greater dissolved P drainage loads than conventional tillage in the MANAGE synthesis \parencite{Christianson2016}. Cover-crop effects on P are inconsistent: a cereal rye cover crop did not significantly reduce drainage discharge or DRP in Illinois \parencite{deOliveira2022}, cover crops tended to raise DRP and TP leaching in lysimeters but not significantly at field drain depth \parencite{Liu2019}, yet modelled winter rye reduced DRP by 16\% (mostly in runoff) \parencite{Grewal2025} and an oat cover crop reduced predicted DRP and TP by 30\% and 54\% \parencite{Askar2021b}. Corn--soybean and corn--soybean--wheat rotations reduced subsurface DRP relative to continuous corn \parencite{Ni2020}, and DRP losses were greater in corn years than soybean years \parencite{Zhang2015}. Simulations indicated moldboard/conventional tillage could reduce drainage DRP and PP (by up to 48\% and 30\% as tillage intensity rose from no-till to moldboard plow) while simultaneously lowering runoff P losses: under one compost scenario, conventional tillage decreased overall runoff P loss by $\sim$50\% and tile-drainage P loss by $\sim$19\% relative to no-till \parencite{Pan2023}, and shifting tillage to spring or injecting fertiliser could cut TP loss by $\sim$10\% and 25\% \parencite{Qi2018}. In snowmelt regions, however, zero tillage and perennial forages can \emph{increase} dissolved P despite reducing erosion---alfalfa forage lost 160\% more TP than cropland, largely via a 221\% rise in dissolved P---so late-fall/winter applications are consistently high-risk \parencite{Baulch2019}.

section: Phosphorus Loss Pathways and Soil Controls
subsection: Preferential Flow, Sediment Mobilisation, and Particulate P Transport
claim_paragraph: At catchment scale, tile drains are quantitatively major sediment pathways. Source-fingerprinting attributed 28--55\% of catchment sediment yield to field drains across UK subcatchments, with eroding channel banks a smaller source (6--12\%) and low overall sediment delivery ratios (14--27\%) indicating substantial in-catchment redeposition \parencite{Walling2002}. In monitored UK drains, topsoil supplied more than two-thirds of the sediment load (70.9--88.6\%), sediment load correlated with drainage volume rather than rainfall, and drains contributed over 50\% of the annual sediment budget in one catchment \parencite{Chapman2005}. Sediment yields ranged 70--978~kg~ha$^{-1}$~yr$^{-1}$ with PP yields 0.04--1.1~kg~ha$^{-1}$~yr$^{-1}$ \parencite{Chapman2005}. Tile-drain sediment flocculates under shear, with maximum flocculation at 0.169~N~m$^{-2}$ and a critical deposition shear stress of 0.056~N~m$^{-2}$, information relevant to its fate in receiving streams \parencite{Stone1997}. Clayey soils exported measurable sediment-associated organic carbon and N (up to 35\% and 20\% of loads) chiefly via subsurface drainage, whereas a sandy soil eroded negligibly and exported only aqueous forms; discharge and soil disturbance (recent plowing) controlled export \parencite{Manninen2023}. At larger scales, non-field sources can dominate: streambanks and ravines supplied 76\% of sediment at a Minnesota outlet \parencite{Dalzell2018}, and streambed storage exceeded annual streambank erosion and suspended-sediment load in an Ohio lake-plain tributary, where streambanks were the largest streambed-sediment source and much sediment had long residence times **[CITATION CHECKED: Williamson2025]**.

section: Manure Application Effects on Soil and Drainage Microbiology
subsection: Overview
claim_paragraph: Manure and other organic amendments sit at the intersection of two functions of subsurface (tile) drainage systems: they enrich soils with nutrients and organic matter, and they introduce fecal microorganisms, resistance genes, hormones, and trace elements that drainage networks can rapidly route to receiving waters. The evidence assembled here establishes several consolidated conclusions. First, the \emph{method} of manure application and the \emph{moisture state} of the soil, rather than manure presence alone, largely govern how much fecal contamination reaches tile drains, with preferential (macropore) flow acting as the dominant transport mechanism \parencite{Truhlar2015,Thiagarajan2007,Collins2007,Ding2021}. Second, manure and organic amendments deliver measurable agronomic and soil-structural benefits---reclamation of saline--sodic soils, higher yields, and, when combined with subsurface drainage and biochar, improved soil physical properties and nitrogen-use efficiency---though some physical benefits are transient \parencite{Qadir2001,Tian2023b,Liu2025f,Xiong2025,Brikmans2025}. Third, drainage systems and their engineered analogues (denitrifying bioreactors, constructed wetlands, reservoirs, and reconstructed oxbows) host distinct and dynamic microbial communities and can substantially attenuate nitrate and pathogen loads **[CITATION CHECKED: Hathaway2015]**. Fourth, drainage water can concentrate and mobilise trace elements---most infamously selenium at Kesterson, but also arsenic, boron, uranium, and micronutrients---with documented consequences for wildlife \parencite{SAIKI1987,Ohlendorf2002,Ryu2010,Gao2007,Tayfur2010,Gul2013}. Finally, subsurface drainage reshapes the ecology of agricultural landscapes, from soil fauna to birds, amphibians, and semi-aquatic species \parencite{Nuutinen2001,Marja2013,Dreyfuss2018,Campbell2023}. This section synthesises the mechanisms and quantified outcomes underpinning each of these lines of evidence.

section: Tile Drainage Influence on Streamflow Dynamics
subsection: Modification of the flow regime
claim_paragraph: Flashiness responds to drainage in a soil- and slope-dependent manner rather than monotonically. A global meta-analysis of 464 watersheds in 13 countries found that stream flashiness (Richards--Baker Index, RBI) was similar overall regardless of tile-drainage extent, but diverged by setting: in flat ($<2$\% slope) watersheds, medium and high drainage extents had higher RBI than low extent, whereas in sloping watersheds low extent had the highest RBI; in low-infiltration soils RBI was higher in lightly drained watersheds, while in high-infiltration soils RBI was similar across classes but the baseflow index (BFI) was higher where drainage was low \parencite{Zhou2025}. Drainage extent itself was positively associated with agricultural land use and clay content and negatively with slope and depth to water table \parencite{Zhou2025}. Field-scale Iowa simulations showed drainage decreased the flashiness index for low-conductivity soils and increased it for high-conductivity soils, thereby homogenizing response across soil types, with a nonlinear, U-shaped dependence on drain spacing and an optimal spacing near 15~m for the Webster soil \parencite{Sloan2016}. Ohio modeling found overall flashiness decreased with tiles, with a nonmonotonic minimum near 50~m spacing \parencite{Rathore2025}. Across 30 Nordic and Baltic catchments, the flashiness index was negatively related to BFI and positively related to the share of agricultural area under artificial drainage and to drainage intensity; computing flashiness from hourly rather than daily discharge increased it by nearly a factor of three on average (range 1.2--4.8) **[CITATION CHECKED: Deelstra2014]**.

section: Nitrate-N Losses Under Drainage Management
subsection: Sources, Transport Pathways, and Transformations
claim_paragraph: Dual-isotope studies indicate that drainage nitrate is often derived largely from organic sources (manure and soil organic matter) via nitrification, with denitrification not always dominant.
